- Capillary leak and hypovolaemia.
- Myocardial depression.
- Relative vasopressin deficiency.

> **Closing point:** Distributive plus cardiac plus volume.

items.title: How do you manage refractory septic shock?
items.q: How do you manage refractory septic shock?
items.a:
- Noradrenaline first line.
- Add vasopressin and hydrocortisone.
- Dobutamine if low output.
- Look for missed source and other causes.

> **Closing point:** Catecholamine-sparing adjuncts.

items.title: What do modern sepsis resuscitation trials teach about volume and perfusion targets?
items.q: What do modern sepsis resuscitation trials teach about volume and perfusion targets?
items.a:
- **Rivers** demonstrated benefit of early structured sepsis resuscitation in its era; **ProCESS, ARISE and ProMISe** found no benefit from mandatory invasive early-goal-directed protocols over improved early standard care.
- **ANDROMEDA-SHOCK:** no statistically significant primary 28-day mortality reduction. **ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 (2025):** improved a hierarchical composite (mortality, vital-support duration, hospital stay); this is not proof of a separate mortality reduction.
- **ARISE FLUIDS (2026):** early pressors/restricted fluids did not improve days alive out of hospital at 90 days versus more fluid/later pressors; pulmonary oedema was less frequent.
- **CLASSIC** and **CLOVERS:** their restrictive strategies did not improve mortality over comparators in studied populations; they do not prove fluid and pressor choices are equivalent in every patient.
- Current **2026 SSC** suggests initial ≥30 mL/kg over 3 hours in sepsis-induced hypoperfusion/shock, **conditional with frequent reassessment** and case-by-case early concurrent pressors for unstable shock.

> **Closing point:** Treat early, use the simplest reliable endpoints and continuously reassess.

items.title: What are the features of anaphylactic shock?
items.q: What are the features of anaphylactic shock?
items.a:
- Sudden hypotension and bronchospasm.
- Rash or oedema.
- ETCO2 falls.
- Triggered by antibiotics, relaxants or latex.

> **Closing point:** Adrenaline first.

items.title: What is the first-line drug for anaphylaxis?
items.q: What is the first-line drug for anaphylaxis?
items.a:
- Monitored adult perioperative dosing (ANZAAG–ANZCA): **10–20 micrograms IV for moderate**, **50–100 micrograms IV for life-threatening** reactions; reassess/repeat and escalate per card. Verify dilution and start infusion for repeated/refractory instability.
- If IV access or monitoring is unavailable, **0.5 mg IM (1 mg/mL)** into the adult anterolateral thigh.
- Prepare an adrenaline infusion early for refractory/recurrent instability; administer appropriate rapid isotonic crystalloid for capillary leak.
- Avoid mistaking an IV preparation for an IM preparation; follow the local crisis card.

> **Closing point:** Treat the grade of reaction; safe adrenaline preparation is crucial.

items.title: What is the difference between neurogenic and spinal shock?
items.q: What is the difference between neurogenic and spinal shock?
items.a:
- Neurogenic: loss of sympathetic tone with hypotension and bradycardia.
- Spinal: loss of reflexes and tone.
- Neurogenic occurs with injury above T6.
- Exclude haemorrhage.

> **Closing point:** Different problems, same injury.

items.title: What blood pressure target applies in acute spinal cord injury?
items.q: What blood pressure target applies in acute spinal cord injury?
items.a:
- For **acute traumatic SCI**, the 2024 guideline weakly suggests augmenting MAP to **at least 75–80 mmHg**, but **not actively beyond 90–95 mmHg**.
- Suggested duration is **3–7 days**, chosen according to physiology and risk; evidence is very low certainty.
- Avoid hypoxaemia and sustained hypotension; do not assume these targets apply to every neurogenic shock patient.
- Choice of vasopressor is individualised; no proven single best agent.

> **Closing point:** Maintain cord perfusion.

items.title: What are the key actions for suspected intraoperative vascular gas embolism?
items.q: What are the key actions for suspected intraoperative vascular gas embolism?
items.a:
- Stop further gas entry/insufflation, desufflate if relevant, stop nitrous oxide and give 100% oxygen.
- Support circulation and use TOE when feasible; aspirate through a suitable existing central line without delaying resuscitation.
- Routine head-down positioning is inappropriate, especially for cerebral arterial embolism; a right-heart gas lock is a specific exception to discuss.
- Seek urgent hyperbaric advice for arterial/cerebral embolism or persistent injury; a normal CT does not exclude it.

items.title: What can cause cardiovascular collapse after tourniquet release or major reperfusion?
items.q: What can cause cardiovascular collapse after tourniquet release or major reperfusion?
items.a: Venous pooling and washout of acid, potassium, CO₂ and vasoactive metabolites may combine with bleeding, anaesthetic vasodilation and myocardial dysfunction. Anticipate the event, check ECG/gas/electrolytes and treat the demonstrated mechanism. Do not assume a single vasopressor or fluid bolus fixes every reperfusion collapse.

items.title: What are the receptor effects of noradrenaline?
items.q: What are the receptor effects of noradrenaline?
items.a:
- Strong alpha-1 vasoconstriction.
- Moderate beta-1 effect.
- Raises MAP and SVR.
- First-line vasopressor.

> **Closing point:** The standard vasopressor.

items.title: What are the effects of adrenaline at different doses?
items.q: What are the effects of adrenaline at different doses?
items.a:
- Low dose: beta-1 and beta-2 effects.
- High dose: alpha-1 vasoconstriction.
- Raises lactate.
- Used in anaphylaxis and arrest.

> **Closing point:** Dose-dependent receptor profile.

items.title: When do you use vasopressin?
items.q: When do you use vasopressin?
items.a:
- Add-on in septic shock and vasoplegia.
- Acts on V1 receptors.
- Often used at ~0.03 units/min as an adjunct, according to local protocol; it is **not** an unconditional fixed dose for every indication.
- Reduces catecholamine need.

> **Closing point:** Catecholamine-sparing.

items.title: What are the risks of dopamine?
items.q: What are the risks of dopamine?
items.a:
- More arrhythmias than noradrenaline.
- SOAP II showed more arrhythmias with dopamine, with a concerning cardiogenic-shock subgroup mortality signal; there was not a significant overall mortality difference.
- Variable receptor effects.
- Rarely first choice.

> **Closing point:** SOAP II changed practice.

items.title: When do you use dobutamine?
items.q: When do you use dobutamine?
items.a:
- Low cardiac output with adequate MAP.
- Septic cardiomyopathy.
- Beta-1 inotropy.
- Can cause hypotension and arrhythmia.

> **Closing point:** Inotrope, not vasopressor.

items.title: What are the effects of milrinone?
items.q: What are the effects of milrinone?
items.a:
- PDE-III inhibitor.
- Inotropy, lusitropy and vasodilatation.
- Reduces pulmonary vascular resistance.
- Renally cleared and may cause hypotension.

> **Closing point:** Inodilator that works despite beta-blockade.

items.title: How can dynamic LV outflow tract obstruction cause shock, and what would you do?
items.q: How can dynamic LV outflow tract obstruction cause shock, and what would you do?
items.a:
- Think **small hyperdynamic LV + SAM + late-peaking LVOT Doppler gradient**, often triggered by low preload, low afterload, tachycardia or catecholamine inotropy.
- Increasing dobutamine/adrenaline can **worsen** obstruction and hypotension despite a vigorous EF.
- Reduce provoking inotropy/tachycardia, cautiously correct true underfilling and **restore afterload** (usually a non-inotropic vasoconstrictor such as phenylephrine or vasopressin); noradrenaline can itself worsen LVOTO in some patients. Consider expert-guided short-acting beta-blockade only after echo diagnosis and perfusion support.
- Use TOE/TTE, ECG and clinical context to distinguish from global pump failure, bleeding and tamponade.

> **Closing point:** A hyperdynamic ventricle can still produce low forward output.

items.title: What is lusitropy and why is it distinct from inotropy?
items.q: What is lusitropy and why is it distinct from inotropy?
items.a:
- **Inotropy** increases the force of contraction; **lusitropy** increases the rate/quality of myocardial relaxation in diastole by improving calcium handling.
- Beta-agonists and PDE3 inhibition can provide positive lusitropy; milrinone combines inotropy/lusitropy with systemic and pulmonary vasodilation.
- In a stiff LV/HFpEF, faster HR, lower SVR or ischaemia may worsen filling despite improved cellular relaxation.
- Preserve sinus rhythm and appropriate diastolic filling time; select medication to correct the actual defect rather than assuming “lusitrope = HFpEF treatment”.

> **Closing point:** Good relaxation is not equivalent to a faster heart.

items.title: How does levosimendan work?
items.q: How does levosimendan work?
items.a:
- Calcium sensitiser.
- K-ATP channel opening.
- Effects last up to a week.
- Evidence is mixed.

> **Closing point:** Calcium sensitiser with long action.

items.title: What is methylene blue used for?
items.q: What is methylene blue used for?
items.a:
- Vasoplegia after bypass.
- Inhibits nitric oxide synthase and guanylate cyclase.
- A specialist vasoplegia regimen may use **1–2 mg/kg over 15–30 min**, with monitoring; not a rapid unqualified push.
- Avoid with serotonergic drugs and G6PD deficiency.

> **Closing point:** Rescue for vasoplegia.

items.title: What are the dangers of extravasation of vasopressors?
items.q: What are the dangers of extravasation of vasopressors?
items.a:
- Tissue necrosis.
- Central access is preferred for prolonged/high-dose treatment, but **appropriately diluted peripheral noradrenaline is acceptable for urgent short-term use with vigilant site monitoring**; do not delay shock treatment while obtaining a central line.
- Use a reliable proximal peripheral line, infusion pump, appropriate concentration and frequent inspection per local policy.
- If extravasation is suspected: **stop the infusion, leave the cannula initially to aspirate (do not flush)**, restart via safe access, elevate/assess the limb and urgently follow the local extravasation pathway, including phentolamine where available.

> **Closing point:** Check the cannula.

items.title: Why might noradrenaline increase MAP but reduce cardiac output?
items.q: Why might noradrenaline increase MAP but reduce cardiac output?
items.a: Venoconstriction can recruit venous blood and improve preload, while arterial constriction supports pressure. But increased LV afterload, RV dysfunction or excessive vasoconstriction can reduce forward flow. Check SV/CO and perfusion, not just MAP; a drug response depends on the starting physiology.

items.title: Which newer septic-shock therapies should not be presented as routine proven treatment?
items.q: Which newer septic-shock therapies should not be presented as routine proven treatment?
items.a: Routine beta-blockade, levosimendan, high-dose IV vitamin C and blood-purification devices lack a general proven outcome benefit; some trials suggest harm. Methylene blue, hydroxocobalamin and angiotensin II are selected specialist options, not a standard ladder for everyone. Keep treatment of specific indications distinct from routine organ protection.

items.title: What are the signs of cardiac tamponade?
items.q: What are the signs of cardiac tamponade?
items.a:
- Beck triad: hypotension, raised JVP, muffled sounds.
- Pulsus paradoxus.
- Falling drain output after cardiac surgery.
- Echo may show chamber collapse, but high right-sided pressure, ventilation or loculated postoperative clot can mask it; absence does not exclude tamponade.

> **Closing point:** Rate of accumulation matters.

items.title: How does traumatic tamponade differ from medical or postoperative tamponade?
items.q: How does traumatic tamponade differ from medical or postoperative tamponade?
items.a:
- **Medical effusion:** image-guided catheter drainage may be definitive; in a large chronic effusion avoid unnecessary rapid complete emptying because of decompression syndrome.
- **Post-cardiac surgery:** loculated clot may compress a chamber with little free fluid; prompt TOE and **surgical re-exploration** are usually preferable when unstable.
- **Penetrating trauma:** presume an active bleeding cardiac injury and arrange **urgent surgical pericardial opening/repair** with haemostatic resuscitation; a needle may not drain clot or stop bleeding.
- Support pressure/oxygenation while definitive decompression is arranged; avoid delaying surgery with serial fluid boluses.

> **Closing point:** Identify the cause of the effusion, not just the presence of fluid.

items.title: What are the haemodynamic goals in tamponade?
items.q: What are the haemodynamic goals in tamponade?
items.a:
- Preserve venous return and avoid unnecessary vasodilation; a **small cautious fluid challenge** may be a bridge if underfilled but repeated fluid is not definitive treatment.
- Maintain compensatory HR/contractility and systemic pressure while arranging **urgent drainage**.
- Avoid vasodilators and positive pressure.
- Drain urgently.

> **Closing point:** Fast, full and tight.

items.title: How should anaesthesia be induced in tamponade?
items.q: How should anaesthesia be induced in tamponade?
items.a:
- Preserve spontaneous ventilation if possible.
- Ketamine with vasopressor ready.
- Surgeon scrubbed and ready.
- Avoid high PEEP.

> **Closing point:** Positive pressure reduces filling.

items.title: What is the technique for ultrasound-guided pericardiocentesis?
items.q: What is the technique for ultrasound-guided pericardiocentesis?
items.a:
- Use ultrasound to select the **shortest safe accessible pericardial fluid pocket** (apical, parasternal or subxiphoid)—not a mandatory subxiphoid track.
- Under asepsis, local anaesthesia and appropriate monitoring, track the needle tip under real-time ultrasound where feasible and aspirate carefully.
- Confirm intrapericardial position by imaging; agitated saline contrast may help if uncertain (blood aspiration alone is insufficient).
- Place a pigtail drain using a safe guidewire technique, relieve haemodynamic obstruction, then monitor for recurrence or decompression syndrome in chronic large effusions.

> **Closing point:** Choose the image-defined safe route; surgery for clotted traumatic/postsurgical blood.

items.title: What are the complications of pericardiocentesis?
items.q: What are the complications of pericardiocentesis?
items.a:
- Coronary or myocardial laceration.
- Arrhythmia and pneumothorax.
- Liver injury.
- Fails in clotted blood.

> **Closing point:** Surgery for clots.

items.title: What is the differential for obstructive shock?
items.q: What is the differential for obstructive shock?
items.a:
- Pulmonary embolism.
- Tension pneumothorax.
- Cardiac tamponade.
- Auto-PEEP and aortocaval compression.

> **Closing point:** Falling ETCO2 is a clue.

items.title: How do you diagnose and treat tension pneumothorax under anaesthesia?
items.q: How do you diagnose and treat tension pneumothorax under anaesthesia?
items.a:
- High airway pressure, unilateral breath sounds, hypotension.
- Stop nitrous oxide.
- Needle or finger decompression.
- Insert a chest drain.

> **Closing point:** Clinical diagnosis; decompress first.

items.title: How do you treat massive pulmonary embolism with shock?
items.q: How do you treat massive pulmonary embolism with shock?
items.a:
- Oxygen and RV support with noradrenaline.
- Avoid fluid overload.
- Thrombolysis or embolectomy.
- ECMO in refractory cases.

> **Closing point:** Support the right ventricle and clear the clot.

items.title: What are the common causes of intraoperative hypotension?
items.q: What are the common causes of intraoperative hypotension?
items.a:
- Anaesthetic vasodilatation and myocardial depression.
- Hypovolaemia and bleeding.
- Cardiac: arrhythmia, ischaemia, valve disease.
- Anaphylaxis, embolism, pneumothorax and sepsis.

> **Closing point:** Work through by mechanism.

items.title: What blood pressure target do you aim for during anaesthesia?
items.q: What blood pressure target do you aim for during anaesthesia?
items.a:
- Avoid sustained severe hypotension. **ACC/AHA 2024:** MAP ≥60–65/SBP ≥90 minimum; **AoA/BIHS 2026:** commonly used higher-risk targets MAP >70 and/or SBP >100. Individualise; do not transfer elective guidance uncritically to emergency shock.
- **“Within 20% of baseline” is not a validated universal requirement.** Consider chronic hypertension and the patient’s autoregulation.
- Higher perfusion pressure may be needed with raised venous, intracranial or compartment pressure, cerebral vascular disease or ongoing ischaemia.
- Assess CO, CRT, lactate trend and organ function, not MAP alone.

> **Closing point:** Avoid severe/prolonged hypotension and individualise to actual perfusion.

items.title: What are the harms of intraoperative hypotension?
items.q: What are the harms of intraoperative hypotension?
items.a:
- Myocardial injury.
- Acute kidney injury.
- Stroke and delirium.
- Deeper/longer episodes are **associated** with greater morbidity and mortality; observational associations do not establish causality for every outcome.

> **Closing point:** Duration and depth both matter.

items.title: Which vasopressors do you use for hypotension after induction?
items.q: Which vasopressors do you use for hypotension after induction?
items.a:
- Phenylephrine 50 to 100 micrograms.
- Ephedrine 3 to 6 mg.
- Noradrenaline infusion.
- Choose by heart rate and cardiac output.

> **Closing point:** Match the drug to the haemodynamic problem.

items.title: How do you assess a patient with severe preoperative hypertension?
items.q: How do you assess a patient with severe preoperative hypertension?
items.a:
- Look for end-organ damage.
- Repeat measurement; check medications.
- Exclude secondary causes.
- Name the guideline: **2026 AoA/BIHS uses clinic <180/120** (home <175/115) to permit planned surgery without documented primary-care normotension; other guidance uses 180/110. Persistent 210/120 before elective surgery warrants deferral/optimisation, and acute organ injury requires emergency treatment.

> **Closing point:** Acute end-organ injury changes urgency; a number alone does not define emergency.

items.title: Which antihypertensives do you continue on the day of surgery?
items.q: Which antihypertensives do you continue on the day of surgery?
items.a:
- Continue beta-blockers.
- Continue calcium-channel blockers.
- **AoA/BIHS 2026 normally continues ACEI/ARB. ACC/AHA 2024 permits omission for 24 h in selected elevated-risk noncardiac surgery for controlled hypertension; continuation is reasonable in HFrEF.** Follow the applicable protocol and document the reason.
- Continue clonidine.

> **Closing point:** Avoid withdrawal rebound.

items.title: How do you blunt the hypertensive response to laryngoscopy?
items.q: How do you blunt the hypertensive response to laryngoscopy?
items.a:
- Opioid such as fentanyl or remifentanil.
- Esmolol or lignocaine.
- Adequate depth of anaesthesia.
- Consider a supraglottic device.

> **Closing point:** Deepen and block.

items.title: What are the secondary causes of hypertension relevant to anaesthesia?
items.q: What are the secondary causes of hypertension relevant to anaesthesia?
items.a:
- Phaeochromocytoma.
- Renal artery stenosis and renal disease.
- Conn syndrome and Cushing syndrome.
- Drugs and pre-eclampsia.

> **Closing point:** Look when it is severe or young.

items.title: How do you treat a hypertensive emergency?
items.q: How do you treat a hypertensive emergency?
items.a:
- Confirm end-organ damage.
- Titratable IV agent: labetalol, GTN or nicardipine.
- In many hypertensive emergencies avoid an abrupt fall (often no more than ~25% MAP initially), **but targets and pace differ in aortic dissection, pregnancy and specific neurological emergencies**.
- Monitor closely with appropriate invasive pressure/critical-care support and treat the organ-specific cause.

> **Closing point:** Slow, controlled reduction.

items.title: Why does hypotension occur after spinal anaesthesia?
items.q: Why does hypotension occur after spinal anaesthesia?
items.a:
- Sympathetic block causes vasodilatation.
- Reduced preload and cardiac accelerator block.
- Bezold–Jarisch reflex.
- Worse in the elderly and hypovolaemic.

> **Closing point:** Vasodilatation plus bradycardia.

items.title: What is the Bezold–Jarisch reflex?
items.q: What is the Bezold–Jarisch reflex?
items.a:
- Underfilled ventricle contracts vigorously.
- Mechanoreceptors trigger vagal response.
- Bradycardia, vasodilatation and hypotension.
- Restore venous return, reduce the provoking stimulus and use atropine/appropriate vasopressor; severe bradycardic shock may need early adrenaline. Give fluid only when indicated and tolerated.

> **Closing point:** A paradoxical vagal reflex.

items.title: How do you manage a hypertensive crisis in phaeochromocytoma surgery?
items.q: How do you manage a hypertensive crisis in phaeochromocytoma surgery?
items.a:
- Stop tumour handling.
- Magnesium, phentolamine, nitroprusside.
- Beta-blocker only after alpha-blockade.
- Prepare for hypotension after ligation.

> **Closing point:** Alpha first.

items.title: How should you approach hypotension and hypertension in PACU?
items.q: How should you approach hypotension and hypertension in PACU?
items.a:
- **Hypotension:** check actual BP/pulse, ABC, depth of sedation, bleeding/drains, vasodilation/neuraxial effects, sepsis, MI/arrhythmia, anaphylaxis, PE and volume loss; use Hb/gas/ECG/echo as appropriate. Treat cause, not just the cuff.
- **Hypertension:** first look for pain, hypoxia, hypercapnia, agitation, urinary retention, shivering, nausea and missed chronic drugs; correct triggers before escalating IV antihypertensives.
- Search for **acute target-organ injury** (myocardial ischaemia, pulmonary oedema, neurological signs or aortic emergency), and adapt BP targets to recent neurovascular/cardiac surgery.
- Reassess ventilation, perfusion and recovery destination after treatment.

> **Closing point:** A hypertensive emergency requires organ injury, not just a very high number.

items.title: How do you manage hypotension in a patient on ACE inhibitors?
items.q: How do you manage hypotension in a patient on ACE inhibitors?
items.a:
- Vasopressin or noradrenaline for refractory vasoplegia.
- Fluid and phenylephrine.
- Review hypotension and reason for ACEI/ARB, rather than making withholding universal; support preload only if appropriate.
- Methylene blue is a specialist rescue agent for selected severe vasoplegia, not routine first-line induction treatment.

> **Closing point:** Renin–angiotensin blockade blunts the response.

items.title: 1. Perforated bowel with persistent shock: anaesthetic plan
items.q: A frail patient with perforated bowel remains shocked despite initial resuscitation and needs urgent laparotomy. Describe your perioperative anaesthetic plan, including how you would reduce the risk of cardiovascular collapse at induction.
items.a:
## Preop — resuscitate while arranging source control

Call senior anaesthesia/surgery/ICU and agree urgency, goals of care and postoperative support. Assess frailty, baseline function, comorbidity and current organ dysfunction; explain material risks without delaying lifesaving treatment. Correct immediately reversible hypoxaemia, severe hypotension, important electrolyte/glucose disturbance and hypothermia. Give timely antimicrobials and expedite source control; do not wait for every lactate or electrolyte value to normalise.

Determine the dominant shock mechanism and any myocardial dysfunction/obstruction. Use measured fluid/blood treatment, dynamic testing when valid and tolerance assessment; avoid repeated empirical litres. Prepare appropriate IV access, crossmatched/emergency blood where indicated and a working noradrenaline infusion for vasoplegia. An arterial line before induction is useful if achievable without harmful delay; verify reliable BP measurement and have a rescue plan.

Treat this as a high aspiration-risk airway; decompress an existing NG tube and plan preoxygenation, airway equipment, suction and an appropriately modified RSI strategy. The aspiration and haemodynamic risks must be considered together.

## Intraop — make induction a coordinated event

Have the surgeon/team ready, vasoactives connected and reliable access confirmed. Reduce and titrate induction doses to illness; ketamine/etomidate are options rather than guarantees of stability. Account for ketamine's possible direct myocardial depression in catecholamine depletion and etomidate's adrenal suppression. Anticipate reduced venous return with positive-pressure ventilation and choose PEEP/pressures balancing oxygenation against RV/preload effects. Avoid awareness when reducing anaesthesia.

After induction, immediately reassess BP, pulse, ECG, ETCO₂, airway pressure and perfusion. If collapse occurs, treat while looking for bleeding, drug effect, anaphylaxis, pump failure or obstruction. Use appropriate monitoring to measure the response to fluid/vasopressor/inotrope interventions; no device algorithm replaces source control. Maintain temperature, glucose/electrolytes, oxygen carriage and haemostasis as required; communicate deterioration early.

## Postop — planned critical care

Choose extubation versus ongoing ventilation from haemodynamic/respiratory status and recovery, not the clock. Arrange ICU/HDU for ongoing shock or major support needs. Provide structured handover of source control, losses/balance, vasoactives, gases and remaining risks. Reassess perfusion, renal function, infection control and fluid de-escalation; monitor for delirium and other organ dysfunction.

> **Evidence anchor:** Blue Book 2025 emergency-laparotomy sections; current SSC guidance. See the source section for review depth and links.

## Self-marking checklist

- Coordinates senior team, urgency, risk/goals of care and ICU plan
- Resuscitates in parallel with antibiotics/source control
- Makes a mechanism-based fluid/vasoactive/monitoring plan
- Balances aspiration risk with induction haemodynamic risk
- Gives titrated induction/ventilation strategy and drug limitations
- Anticipates and treats collapse without permitting awareness
- Includes postoperative organ support, handover and reassessment

items.title: 2. Balanced crystalloid, saline and colloid in hypovolaemic shock
items.q: Compare the use of balanced crystalloids, 0.9% saline and synthetic colloids in the resuscitation of a patient with hypovolaemic shock.
items.a:
## Properties

- **0.9% saline**: Na and Cl 154 mmol/L each, strong ion difference zero; large volumes cause **hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis**. The chloride load, rather than bag pH, explains this. Kidney effects vary by population/trial; avoid claiming universal AKI harm. Useful for **chloride-depletion alkalosis**; commonly preferred for initial isotonic resuscitation in **TBI**. Hypertonic therapy for intracranial hypertension is a separate indication.
- **Balanced crystalloids** (Hartmann's/lactated Ringer's, Plasma-Lyte): closer to plasma, with buffers (lactate, acetate, gluconate). Hartmann's is slightly hypotonic (not ideal for TBI); Plasma-Lyte is isotonic. Potassium content (4–5 mmol/L) does not automatically contraindicate use in renal impairment; still consider measured K, excretory function and acid–base status. Isotonicity alone does not establish the best fluid for TBI.
- **Synthetic colloids** (hydroxyethyl starch, gelatin): may provide greater initial plasma expansion per volume; capillary leak limits retention and no reliable universal crystalloid:colloid replacement ratio applies. Each has toxicity.

## Evidence

- **SPLIT, SMART, PLUS**: balanced crystalloids reduced major adverse kidney events in some (SMART), though effects on mortality were small or absent (PLUS).
- **Starches:** **CHEST** increased RRT use without a statistically significant mortality difference; **6S** found increased mortality and RRT in severe sepsis. CRYSTMAS is not interchangeable proof of either outcome. Avoid HES in critically ill/septic patients.
- **Gelatin**: anaphylaxis risk, coagulopathy.
- **SAFE**: albumin was equivalent to saline overall.
- **Resuscitation of haemorrhage**: blood is the preferred replacement; large crystalloid volumes cause dilution, coagulopathy, acidosis, and hypothermia.

## Conclusion

Use **balanced crystalloid** first, in measured boluses with reassessment; **saline** for specific indications; **avoid starches**; use **blood products** early for haemorrhage.

> **Evidence anchor:** Fluids in sepsis (2026); CHEST; current SSC guidance. See the source section for review depth and links.

## Self-marking checklist

- Composition and acid–base effects of saline versus balanced fluid
- Appropriate fluid for TBI and hypochloraemia
- Colloid properties and rationale
- Starch harm evidence (CHEST, 6S)
- Balanced fluid trial evidence
- Gelatin and albumin points
- Role of blood in haemorrhage
- A reasoned conclusion

items.title: 3. Classification and resuscitation of haemorrhagic shock
items.q: Discuss the classification and resuscitation of haemorrhagic shock in a 35-year-old patient.
items.a:
## Classification (ATLS)

- **Class I**: under 15% blood loss (under 750 mL); normal vital signs.
- **Class II**: 15 to 30%; tachycardia, narrowed pulse pressure, normal BP.
- **Class III**: 30 to 40% (1500 to 2000 mL); hypotension, tachycardia over 120, confusion, low urine output.
- **Class IV**: over 40%; profound shock, lethargy, imminent arrest.
Blood volume is about **70 mL/kg** in an adult. The classification is a guide only: young fit patients compensate until late; beta-blockers mask tachycardia; elderly patients decompensate early.

## Pathophysiology

Reduced preload gives reduced cardiac output, sympathetic activation (tachycardia, vasoconstriction), renin–angiotensin, ADH, and **lethal triad** of hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy.

## Resuscitation

- **1.** **Stop the bleeding**: direct pressure, tourniquet, splint pelvis, surgery or interventional radiology; the priority is **source control**.
- **2.** **Access** (two large-bore cannulae or intraosseous), arterial line, send bloods (including group and crossmatch, FBC, coagulation, fibrinogen, gas, lactate), viscoelastic testing.
- **3.** **Fluids**: avoid large volumes of crystalloid; **permissive hypotension** (approximately SBP 80–90 in selected uncontrolled traumatic bleeding; avoid deliberate hypotension with important TBI or spinal cord injury and individualise to organ perfusion) until bleeding is controlled.
- **4.** **Blood products**: **local major haemorrhage protocol**, using balanced components initially (e.g. 1:1:1 RBC:plasma:adult platelet-dose equivalents, not individual platelet units), or an established factor-concentrate strategy, then laboratory/viscoelastic-guided treatment, **tranexamic acid** (1 g over 10 minutes then 1 g over 8 hours, within 3 hours), calcium, fibrinogen or cryoprecipitate, PCC when indicated.
- **5.** **Prevent the lethal triad**: warm fluids and patient, correct acidosis by restoring perfusion, check ionised calcium and potassium.
- **6.** **Vasopressors** as bridging if life-threatening hypotension persists (with volume), and **cell salvage** where possible.
- **7.** **Monitor** response: lactate, base excess, urine output, haemoglobin and clotting.

## Self-marking checklist

- States ATLS classes and the limits of the classification
- Compensatory physiology
- Source control as priority
- Permissive hypotension and its exceptions
- Massive transfusion ratios and tranexamic acid
- Calcium, fibrinogen, and viscoelastic guidance
- Lethal triad prevention
- Monitoring endpoints

items.title: 4. Gastroenteritis in a lethargic 3-year-old
items.q: A 3-year-old child with gastroenteritis is lethargic with a heart rate of 170 and capillary refill of 5 seconds. Discuss assessment and fluid resuscitation.
items.a:
## Assessment

Children **compensate until late** (BP may remain preserved until substantial volume loss), so use **perfusion signs**: capillary refill over 3 seconds, tachycardia, cool peripheries, weak pulses, lethargy, reduced urine output, sunken eyes, and reduced skin turgor. This child has **shock with concerning hypoperfusion** (lethargy, tachycardia, CRT 5 seconds). Without BP and further assessment, do not assert hypotensive/decompensated shock solely from the supplied findings.
Investigations: glucose (hypoglycaemia), gas and lactate, electrolytes (hyper- or hyponatraemia), urea and creatinine, ketones.

## Resuscitation

- **1.** ABC, oxygen, access (IV or **intraosseous** if not within 60–90 seconds).
- **2.** **Bolus 10 to 20 mL/kg of isotonic fluid** (balanced crystalloid or 0.9% saline) over 5 to 10 minutes; **reassess after each**, repeat if still shocked; if repeated boluses are needed, urgently reconsider ongoing losses, sepsis, cardiac function and fluid tolerance before further volume.
- **3.** Correct **hypoglycaemia** (2 mL/kg 10% dextrose).
- **Deficit:** estimate from recent weight change and clinical course; account for resuscitation already given, sodium abnormality and rate of losses. Write **separate maintenance and ongoing-loss prescriptions**; adjust correction timing to physiology and local paediatric protocol (especially chronic hypernatraemia).
- **5.** For the unwell/NPO child, use an appropriate **isotonic maintenance solution with glucose as indicated**, checking glucose frequently. Healthy older children having short operations do not routinely need intraoperative glucose. Stress-related ADH may require a lower postoperative maintenance rate; avoid hypotonic solutions.
- **6.** **Electrolytes**: correct potassium and sodium slowly.
- **7.** **Monitoring**: heart rate, capillary refill, urine output, weight, and electrolytes.

## Pitfalls

Fluid overload, hypoglycaemia, missed sepsis, and rapid sodium correction.

> **Evidence anchor:** Paediatric fluids (2023); RCH assessment/resuscitation guidance. See the source section for review depth and links.

## Self-marking checklist

- Perfusion-based assessment
- Recognises clinical shock; does not assume hypotension from missing BP
- Bolus volume, fluid type and reassessment
- Intraosseous access
- Glucose
- Deficit and maintenance calculation
- Avoids hypotonic fluids
- Electrolyte correction rate

items.title: 5. Bowel obstruction with nasogastric losses and alkalosis
items.q: A 62-year-old patient with bowel obstruction has had 1.5 L/day of nasogastric losses, is tachycardic and oliguric, and has hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis. Discuss perioperative resuscitation, maintenance and ongoing-loss replacement.
items.a:
## Physiological diagnosis

Persistent vomiting/NG suction causes **loss of water, sodium, chloride, gastric HCl and often potassium**. This produces extracellular volume depletion with **hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis**, secondary K loss and potentially AKI. Hypotension and oliguria may reflect poor forward flow, but interpretation needs serial clinical examination.

## Initial assessment and resuscitation

- ABCDE, actual BP/pulse waveform, perfusion (CRT, mental state, urine), focused loss history, abdominal examination and possible sepsis/ischaemia.
- Establish IV access; measure blood gas, K, Cl, Na, Mg, glucose, creatinine, lactate and Hb; ECG if hypokalaemia.
- If hypoperfused, give a **small 250–500 mL isotonic crystalloid aliquot** (less if limited cardiac reserve), then reassess SV/MAP, CRT, respiratory signs and congestion; repeat only if beneficial and safe.
- Initial perfusion resuscitation can use balanced fluid, but **0.9% saline may be specifically useful to replace sustained gastric chloride loss**, with separate carefully prescribed K replacement. Avoid treating chloride-depletion alkalosis with endless chloride-poor fluid.

## Write three prescriptions, not one

- **1.** **Resuscitation:** short-term aliquots for current hypoperfusion with a stated response endpoint.
- **2.** **Maintenance:** actual daily water, sodium, potassium and glucose requirements, subtracting oral/enteral intake and medication-infusion volumes and adjusting for renal function.
- **3.** **Ongoing measured losses:** replace NG aspirate according to **measured volume and electrolyte pattern**, reassessing frequent electrolytes and acid–base; never add K indiscriminately in oliguria.

## Anaesthesia and surgery

- Elective procedures: correct major dehydration, AKI and dangerous K disturbances first. For suspected strangulation/ischaemia, **resuscitate concurrently with urgent surgery**.
- Anticipate aspiration, haemodynamic collapse at induction and worsened venous return with positive pressure; decompress stomach, plan airway, monitor and have vasoactives prepared.
- Reassess after surgery for ongoing NG losses, infection and fluid overload.

> **Evidence anchor:** Paediatric/adult principles distinguished; current Set 1 nonhaemorrhagic-loss teaching. See the source section for review depth and links.

## Self-marking checklist

- Explains chloride/HCl and volume losses causing alkalosis and K depletion
- Assesses perfusion, organ injury and electrolytes before fluids
- Uses titrated isotonic resuscitation with a specified reassessment endpoint
- Distinguishes resuscitation, maintenance and ongoing-loss prescriptions
- Recognises when chloride-rich saline and monitored K replacement are appropriate
- Individualises operative timing to source control and physiological stability
- Mentions aspiration, induction risk and postoperative monitoring

items.title: 6. Falling ETCO₂ and hypotension during laparoscopy
items.q: A patient becomes acutely hypotensive with a falling ETCO2 during laparoscopic surgery. Discuss your approach to the differential diagnosis of obstructive shock.
items.a:
## Obstructive shock

Impaired cardiac output due to **physical obstruction of flow** which may cause secondary RV/LV dysfunction; filling pressures depend on the obstruction and coexisting volume status. Main causes:
- **Pulmonary embolism** (thrombus, air, fat, CO2, amniotic fluid, cement).
- **Tension pneumothorax** (barotrauma, central line, laparoscopic CO2 tracking).
- **Cardiac tamponade**.
- **Auto-PEEP** (dynamic hyperinflation).
- **Aortocaval compression** (pregnancy, pneumoperitoneum).
- Severe **pulmonary hypertension** or right ventricular failure.

## Approach

- **1.** **Recognise** the pattern: hypotension with **fall in ETCO2**, raised CVP/JVP, hypoxaemia, tachycardia.
- **2.** **Immediate steps**: 100% oxygen, **stop insufflation/desufflate**, briefly disconnect the circuit **if severe dynamic hyperinflation is suspected**, allowing passive exhalation, exclude hypovolaemia and anaphylaxis, ask for help.
- **3.** **Look for specific causes**:
  - Tension pneumothorax: unilateral breath sounds, high airway pressures, tracheal shift → **needle or finger decompression, then chest drain**.
  - Gas embolism: sudden ETCO₂ change/collapse and TOE bubbles; a mill-wheel murmur is insensitive. **Stop gas entry/desufflate, stop N₂O, give 100% O₂ and support circulation.** Aspirate via an appropriately positioned **existing** central line if feasible; do not delay resuscitation to insert one. Routine head-down positioning is not recommended, especially with cerebral arterial embolism; consider left lateral/head-down only for a suspected right-heart gas lock when feasible. Urgently discuss hyperbaric treatment for arterial/cerebral embolism or persistent neurological/cardiopulmonary injury.
  - High-risk PE: RV strain supports but does not prove diagnosis. Activate senior PE/cardiothoracic help; UFH and reperfusion selection depend on active bleeding and recent surgery. **Systemic thrombolysis, catheter treatment or surgical embolectomy** are options; surgery/active bleeding can favour mechanical reperfusion. Alteplase 100 mg over 2 h is a recognised adult high-risk PE regimen; arrest dosing varies by protocol—do not present a 50-mg bolus as universal. In arrest, use the current resuscitation algorithm and consider prolonged CPR after thrombolysis.
  - Tamponade: echo.
- **4.** **Point-of-care echo** is the quickest discriminator (RV dilatation, effusion, hypovolaemic collapse).
- **5.** **Haemodynamic support**: noradrenaline, avoid excessive fluid in RV failure, inhaled pulmonary vasodilators (nitric oxide), ECMO in refractory cases.

## Self-marking checklist

- Defines obstructive shock
- Lists causes
- Recognises the ETCO2 clue
- Immediate manoeuvres
- Cause-specific treatment
- Role of echocardiography
- RV support strategies
- Rescue (thrombolysis, ECMO)

items.title: 7. Dynamic hyperinflation with sudden collapse
items.q: During ventilation of a patient with severe obstructive lung disease, the MAP and ETCO₂ suddenly fall, airway pressures rise and expiratory flow never returns to zero. Discuss diagnosis and immediate management.
items.a:
## Diagnosis and mechanism

The pattern suggests **dynamic hyperinflation/auto-PEEP causing obstructive shock**: gas trapping increases intrathoracic pressure, impairs systemic venous return, may impair RV ejection and reduces cardiac output. It can lead to profound hypotension/PEA. However, check for **tube/circuit obstruction, bronchospasm, tension pneumothorax, endobronchial intubation, PE and haemorrhage**.

## Immediate actions

- **1.** Call for help, assess the actual pulse/rhythm, give oxygen and verify airway/capnography; stop surgical stimulation where possible.
- **2.** **Relieve trapped gas immediately if severe collapse**: briefly disconnect the circuit under controlled clinical conditions to allow passive exhalation, while preparing resuscitation. Avoid continuing excessive manual bagging.
- **3.** Reduce RR/minute ventilation as safe, **allow prolonged expiration**, reduce VT where appropriate and adjust inspiratory flow/I:E ratio. Use the flow-time waveform to confirm end-expiratory flow returns to zero. Titrate external PEEP carefully, not automatically high.
- **4.** Treat bronchospasm (inhaled bronchodilators, appropriate depth, other cause-specific therapy), correct hypoxaemia/acidosis and support circulation with an appropriate vasoactive agent as a bridge.
- **5.** If unilateral signs/lung US suggest **tension pneumothorax**, decompress immediately; do not assume all high-pressure states are auto-PEEP.

## Reassessment

Evaluate airway and lung mechanics, pulse pressure, ETCO₂, ABG, echo when appropriate and response to ventilator changes. More IV fluid is **not** definitive relief of mechanical obstruction.

## Self-marking checklist

- Identifies dynamic hyperinflation/auto-PEEP and its effect on venous return/CO
- Recognises airway pressures, flow-time waveform, ETCO₂ and hypotension pattern
- Excludes tube/circuit problems and tension pneumothorax rapidly
- Describes brief controlled circuit disconnect when severe gas-trapping collapse occurs
- Adjusts RR/VT/expiratory time and treats bronchospasm
- Gives appropriate perfusion support without blind fluids
- Reassesses perfusion, ventilator mechanics and alternative causes

items.title: 8. Intraoperative anaphylaxis with refractory hypotension
items.q: Describe your management of severe intraoperative anaphylaxis presenting with refractory hypotension.
items.a:
## Recognition

Sudden hypotension, tachycardia, bronchospasm, rising airway pressure, falling ETCO2, rash or oedema, often within minutes of an intravenous drug (rocuronium, antibiotics, chlorhexidine, latex, patent blue dye, sugammadex).

## Immediate management (ANZAAG)

- **1.** **Stop the trigger** (drug, latex, colloid), call for help, 100% oxygen, secure the airway, and stop the surgery if possible.
- **2.** **Adrenaline:** with IV access/monitoring and an anaesthetist, ANZAAG–ANZCA adult card: **moderate reaction 10–20 micrograms IV; life-threatening reaction 50–100 micrograms IV**, reassess/repeat every 1–2 min and escalate per card. The severe stem requires the latter starting range, not a universal low-dose regimen. Use **1 mg in 10 mL = 100 micrograms/mL** with concentration double-checks. If no IV access/haemodynamic monitoring or while awaiting infusion, **0.5 mg IM (1 mg/mL) lateral thigh**, repeat after 5 min if needed. Start a titrated infusion early after repeated boluses (card example **0.05–0.5 micrograms/kg/min**). In arrest, use **1 mg IV/IO** and the local anaphylaxis/arrest card; the timing on the ANZAAG card and generic ALS differs, so use the applicable protocol explicitly.
- **3.** **Fluid:** rapid IV isotonic crystalloid (often 20 mL/kg aliquots for severe vasodilatory capillary leak), reassessing fluid need, oxygenation and haemodynamics repeatedly.
- **4.** **Refractory shock:** check trigger removal, IV delivery and diagnosis; use an adrenaline infusion and consider **noradrenaline/vasopressin**, **glucagon in beta-blockade**, and specialist ECMO where appropriate. Methylene blue is exceptional rescue, not routine: assess serotonin-toxicity risk with serotonergic drugs and haemolysis risk in G6PD deficiency.
- **5.** **Bronchospasm**: salbutamol, volatile agent, ketamine; **ventilation** with long expiratory time.
- **6.** **Adjuncts** (not first-line): antihistamine, hydrocortisone.
- **7.** **Monitoring**: arterial line, ECG, ABG; ICU admission.

## After

Take tryptase as soon as practicable after stabilisation, obtain a further acute sample according to the ANZAAG protocol (often 1–2 h after onset) and a **baseline** sample ≥24 h after resolution/at follow-up; document drugs/times, counsel the patient and arrange formal allergy referral. Sampling must not delay resuscitation.

## Self-marking checklist

- Recognition and common triggers
- Stop trigger and call for help
- Adrenaline route, doses and infusion
- Fluid resuscitation
- Refractory shock options
- Bronchospasm management
- Tryptase sampling and referral
- ICU monitoring

items.title: 9. Hypotension after induction for hip fracture
items.q: A 70-year-old man with hypertension develops a blood pressure of 70/40 mmHg 20 minutes after induction of general anaesthesia for a hip fracture. Discuss your assessment and management.
items.a:
## Immediate response

Call for help if needed, confirm the reading (re-zero, check cuff), reduce excessive volatile/propofol while maintaining appropriate anaesthesia and awareness prevention, give **100% oxygen**, check the airway, ventilation and ECG, and tell the surgeon.

## Differential diagnosis (by mechanism)

- **Anaesthetic**: relative overdose, vasodilatation, reduced sympathetic tone, drug error, high spinal.
- **Hypovolaemia**: dehydration, bleeding (fracture, occult), fasting.
- **Cardiac**: arrhythmia, ischaemia, heart failure, valve disease (aortic stenosis), tamponade.
- **Obstructive**: tension pneumothorax, pulmonary embolism, fat or cement embolism, auto-PEEP.
- **Distributive**: anaphylaxis, sepsis, adrenal insufficiency, neurogenic.
- **Mechanical**: positioning, surgical compression of the IVC.

## Management

- **1.** **Treat the cause** as you diagnose it.
- **2.** **Bridge according to physiology:** titrate **phenylephrine 50–100 micrograms IV**, **ephedrine 3–6 mg IV** (repeat to response), or **noradrenaline infusion initially around 0.02–0.1 micrograms/kg/min** for vasodilation according to HR and cardiac output; these are adult starting examples, not maximum doses; consider a small 250–500 mL isotonic fluid aliquot **only with likely underfilling and acceptable tolerance**, and blood replacement/haemostasis for haemorrhage.
- **3.** **Targeted tests**: ECG for ischaemia, arterial blood gas, haemoglobin, point-of-care echocardiography, and ETCO2.
- **4.** **Anaphylaxis**: adrenaline. **Arrhythmia**: cardiovert or treat. **Haemorrhage**: transfusion.
- **5.** **Avoid sustained severe hypotension**: 2024 ACC/AHA uses MAP ≥60–65/SBP ≥90 as a minimum; the 2026 AoA/BIHS guidance describes **MAP >70 and/or SBP >100** as commonly used higher-risk targets. For this emergency patient individualise to perfusion, baseline disease and procedure; neither value proves adequate flow. The “within 20% of baseline” rule is **not an established universal target**. Persistent low SV/CRT/ETCO₂ is important even if BP improves.

## Prevention and follow-up

Titrated induction, haemodynamic rescue drugs ready, an arterial line when justified by risk, and correction of volume deficits. **Review ACEI/ARB continuation/withholding individually** by indication and procedure. Consider ECG/troponin surveillance for sustained severe hypotension or suspected myocardial injury, according to risk.

> **Evidence anchor:** AoA/BIHS perioperative BP guideline (2026). See the source section for review depth and links.

## Self-marking checklist

- Immediate checks (reading, oxygen, reduce anaesthetic)
- Differential by mechanism
- Specific life-threatening causes (anaphylaxis, PE, tension pneumothorax, ischaemia)
- Vasopressor and fluid choices with doses
- Avoids sustained severe hypotension; individualises MAP to perfusion and baseline disease
- Investigations (ECG, gas, echo)
- Communication with the surgeon
- Consequences and prevention

items.title: 10. Hypotension and bradycardia after spinal anaesthesia
items.q: An 80-year-old woman becomes severely hypotensive and bradycardic 10 minutes after a spinal anaesthetic for hip surgery. Discuss the causes and management.
items.a:
## Mechanism

- **Sympathetic block** (sympathetic outflow T1–L2; cardiac accelerator fibres principally T1–T4): arterial and venous **vasodilatation**, reduced preload and SVR, plus loss of cardiac accelerator tone causing **bradycardia**.
- **Bezold–Jarisch reflex**: vigorous contraction of an underfilled ventricle activates cardiac mechanoreceptors, producing paradoxical bradycardia, vasodilatation and hypotension.
- **High or total spinal**: loss of consciousness, apnoea.
- **Contributing factors**: elderly (reduced reserve, stiff ventricle), hypovolaemia (fracture), sedation, positioning, cement implantation (BCIS), anaphylaxis, local anaesthetic toxicity, drug interactions, and dose too large.

## Management

- **1.** **Call for help**, 100% oxygen, lie flat and elevate the legs, check the block height.
- **2.** **Vasopressor**: **phenylephrine 50 to 100 micrograms or noradrenaline** (if HR is not low) or **ephedrine 6 to 12 mg**; **atropine 0.6 mg IV** as a local perioperative adult starting example (repeat/escalate under the current bradycardia algorithm); do not delay adrenaline for severe bradycardic shock; **adrenaline 10 to 50 micrograms** for severe bradycardia with hypotension, escalating early in profound shock.
- **3.** **Fluids**: bolus warmed isotonic fluid (250 to 500 mL).
- **4.** **Airway and ventilation** support if high block; intubate if needed.
- **5.** **Cardiac arrest**: immediate CPR/ALS; adult **adrenaline 1 mg IV/IO according to the arrest algorithm**, distinct from microgram boluses when a pulse remains.
- **6.** **Reassess** for other causes (haemorrhage, PE, ischaemia, anaphylaxis).

## Prevention

Reduced-dose hyperbaric bupivacaine (e.g. 7.5 to 10 mg) in the elderly, prophylactic **noradrenaline or phenylephrine infusion**, slow-onset techniques, correct hypovolaemia, avoid combined sedation, and an arterial line in high-risk patients.

> **Evidence anchor:** AoA/BIHS BP targets (2026); mechanism-specific Set 1 teaching. See the source section for review depth and links.

## Self-marking checklist

- Mechanisms (sympathetic block, Bezold–Jarisch)
- High or total spinal considerations
- Risk factors in the elderly
- Stepwise drug management with doses
- Fluids and positioning
- Airway support
- Differential for other causes
- Prevention strategies

items.title: 11. Severe preoperative hypertension (210/120) before elective surgery
items.q: A 58-year-old woman with untreated hypertension has a blood pressure of 210/120 mmHg in the preoperative holding bay before elective surgery. Discuss your approach.
items.a:
## Preop — assessment

- **Is there acute end-organ injury?** Chest pain, ECG changes, neurological signs, headache, visual change, pulmonary oedema, renal impairment (hypertensive emergency). If yes, **cancel surgery** and treat in a monitored area.
- **Causes**: untreated essential hypertension (commonest), missed medication, pain, anxiety, full bladder, withdrawal (clonidine, beta-blockers, alcohol), **secondary causes** (phaeochromocytoma, renal artery stenosis, Conn's, Cushing's, pre-eclampsia, drugs).
- **Repeat the measurement** (correct cuff size, rest), review the history, medications, and previous readings.

## Decision

- **Name the applicable guideline:** the 2026 Association of Anaesthetists/BIHS update permits planned surgery without documented primary-care normotension when clinic BP is **<180/120 mmHg** (home/ambulatory <175/115). The familiar **180/110** threshold appears in other guidance and should not be presented as universal. Apply the guideline within its scope: planned adult surgery, with specialist exceptions including obstetrics/endocrine surgery and cardiac intraoperative management; elective cardiac preassessment is discussed separately in the full text. It is not an emergency-surgery postponement rule.
- **This patient at 210/120:** repeat carefully; for elective surgery defer for assessment and controlled optimisation, particularly if persistent. Acute organ injury requires emergency treatment. Surgery urgency and local policy still determine the final decision; do not rapidly lower asymptomatic BP simply to get below a number.
- **Weigh** urgency, patient's wishes, and the chance of getting control in the time available.

## Management

- Treat pain and anxiety; continue appropriate beta-blockers/other essential chronic medications, and explain the guideline difference: **2026 AoA/BIHS normally continues ACEI/ARB**, whereas **2024 ACC/AHA allows omission 24 h before selected elevated-risk noncardiac surgery for controlled hypertension**, with continuation reasonable in HFrEF. Follow the applicable protocol and document the indication and hypotension risk.
- If proceeding and treatment is necessary, use a titrated, cause-appropriate agent (e.g. labetalol, nicardipine, GTN or esmolol). In **hypertensive emergency** avoid precipitous reduction; a general initial ≤25% MAP reduction rule has important **aortic, obstetric and neurovascular exceptions**. Asymptomatic high BP does not automatically require urgent IV reduction.
## Intraop — if proceeding

Smooth induction, adequate anaesthetic depth/analgesia and cause-appropriate blunting of laryngoscopy; choose invasive monitoring according to risk. Avoid both severe hypertension and treatment-induced hypotension.

## Postop

Treat pain, hypoxia, hypercapnia, shivering and urinary retention; plan medication resumption and follow-up with the GP for long-term BP control.

> **Evidence anchor:** AoA/BIHS perioperative BP guideline and correction (2026); ACC/AHA distinctions. See the source section for review depth and links.

## Self-marking checklist

- Looks for end-organ injury
- Reasons for severe hypertension and secondary causes
- Repeat measurement
- Decision threshold to proceed or defer
- Acute drug options and cautious lowering
- Continues beta-blockers; ACE inhibitor/ARB policy
- Intraoperative plan to blunt responses
- Follow-up and referral

items.title: 12. Sustained intraoperative hypertension (230/120)
items.q: During general anaesthesia, a patient develops sustained BP 230/120 mmHg and HR 115/min after a period of previously stable observations. Discuss assessment and management.
items.a:
## Immediate assessment

Confirm the cuff/arterial reading and trend; check HR/rhythm, oxygenation, ETCO₂ and ventilation. Tell the surgeon and request a brief pause if stimulation may be contributing. Confirm anaesthetic delivery (vapouriser, circuit, IV access, infusion line/pump), depth and analgesia; hypertension may accompany **accidental awareness**, but absence of movement under paralysis does not establish adequate hypnosis.

## Differential and urgency

Common causes include painful stimulation/light anaesthesia, hypoxia/hypercapnia, bladder distension, positioning, pneumoperitoneum and drug error or excessive vasopressor. Consider missed/withdrawn medication and, in context, catecholamine excess, raised ICP or autonomic dysreflexia. Assess for acute myocardial ischaemia/arrhythmia, pulmonary oedema, neurological/aortic pathology where relevant and surgical bleeding risk. Chronic hypertension alone does not establish an acute emergency; the abrupt trajectory and signs of injury determine urgency.

## Treatment

Correct the cause while controlling dangerous pressure: restore reliable hypnosis/analgesia, correct gas exchange and stop inadvertent pressor delivery. Avoid simply masking inadequate anaesthesia with a beta-blocker. If BP remains dangerously elevated, choose a short-acting, titratable agent matched to the physiology. Examples include cautious **esmolol** for excessive tachycardic sympathetic drive when cardiac function permits, **nicardipine** for arterial vasodilation, or **GTN** for associated ischaemia/pulmonary oedema. Check contraindications—beta-blockade can be harmful in low-output failure, important conduction disease/bronchospasm or unopposed catecholamine excess.

Use close BP/ECG monitoring and consider an arterial line for sustained severe instability. Avoid overshoot; many hypertensive emergencies use no more than about 20–25% MAP reduction initially, but acute aortic and specific neurovascular/obstetric syndromes have their own targets. Seek help and an organ-specific pathway if injury is suspected.

## Postop

Document the episode/cause, treatment and response; assess for myocardial or other organ injury where indicated and arrange an appropriate monitored recovery destination. If awareness is possible, follow the structured assessment, explanation and follow-up pathway. Communicate medication and long-term BP plans.

> **Evidence anchor:** Hypertensive emergencies (2024); AoA/BIHS BP guidance (2026). See the source section for review depth and links.

## Self-marking checklist

- Confirms the measurement and accompanying physiological changes
- Checks anaesthetic delivery/awareness, analgesia and ventilation
- Gives likely causes plus targeted dangerous alternatives
- Assesses organ injury and surgical consequences
- Corrects the cause before simply masking the response
- Selects titratable treatment with contraindications and avoids overshoot
- Includes escalation, postoperative review and possible-awareness follow-up

items.title: 13. Phaeochromocytoma hypertensive crisis
items.q: A patient with a known phaeochromocytoma develops a hypertensive crisis (BP 250/140 mmHg) during anaesthesia. Discuss the causes and management.
items.a:
## Causes

- **Catecholamine release** from tumour manipulation, induction, intubation, pneumoperitoneum, or positioning.
- **Inadequate alpha-blockade**, drugs that trigger release (ketamine, ephedrine, metoclopramide, suxamethonium, droperidol, glucagon), and light anaesthesia.
- Other causes: awareness, pain, hypercarbia, hypoxia, full bladder, malignant hyperthermia, and drug error.

## Management

- **1.** **Tell the surgeon to stop manipulation.** Deepen anaesthesia, check oxygenation and ventilation.
- **2.** **Short-acting vasodilators**:
  - **Magnesium sulphate** 2 to 4 g bolus then 1 to 2 g/h (inhibits catecholamine release and vasodilates).
  - **Phentolamine** 1 to 5 mg boluses.
  - **Sodium nitroprusside** (0.5 to 10 micrograms/kg/min) or **GTN**.
  - **Remifentanil** or **esmolol** (only after alpha-blockade, otherwise unopposed alpha effect can worsen it).
  - Clevidipine or nicardipine infusion.
- **3.** **Tachycardia/arrhythmia**: esmolol, lidocaine, amiodarone.
- **4.** Use an **arterial line**; then manage the **hypotensive phase** after tumour venous ligation (fluids, noradrenaline, vasopressin, and watch for hypoglycaemia).

## Prevention

Preoperative alpha-blockade (phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin) for at least 10 to 14 days, volume loading, then beta-blockade; blood pressure below 130/80 supine, and avoid the triggers. Aim for adequate salt/fluid intake if tolerated; avoid indiscriminate loading in cardiomyopathy. Beta-blockade is added only if tachycardia requires it after alpha control, not automatically for every patient.

> **Evidence anchor:** Hypertensive emergencies (2024); current Set 1 endocrine application. See the source section for review depth and links.

## Self-marking checklist

- Causes during anaesthesia
- Stop stimulation and deepen anaesthesia
- Magnesium, phentolamine, nitroprusside doses
- Beta-blocker caution
- Arrhythmia management
- Post-ligation hypotension
- Preoperative blockade
- Drugs to avoid

items.title: 14. Bedside assessment and classification of shock
items.q: Outline your approach to the clinical assessment of a patient in shock and how you would classify the type of shock at the bedside.
items.a:
## Definition

**Shock** is acute circulatory failure with **inadequate cellular oxygen delivery and/or utilisation relative to metabolic demand**, producing cellular dysfunction. Hypotension is common but not required.

## Assessment

**History**: onset, trauma, bleeding, sepsis symptoms, chest pain, drugs, allergies, cardiac and pregnancy history.
**Examination**
- **Perfusion**: skin temperature and capillary refill, mottling, mental state, urine output, peripheral pulses.
- **Haemodynamics**: heart rate, BP, pulse pressure, JVP, heart sounds, lung fields (oedema, wheeze, unilateral signs), abdomen and wounds, and rashes.
- **Temperature**, respiratory rate.

**Monitoring and tests**: arterial line, ECG, lactate and gas, haemoglobin, troponin, cultures, coagulation, renal and liver tests, chest X-ray, **point-of-care echocardiography** (RUSH protocol: pump, tank, pipes), dynamic indices (pulse pressure variation, passive leg raise).

## Bedside classification

| Type | Features |
|---|---|
| **Hypovolaemic** | Cold, flat veins, low JVP, history of loss |
| **Cardiogenic** | Cold, raised JVP, crackles, S3 |
| **Obstructive** | Raised JVP, absent breath sounds or pulsus paradoxus |
| **Distributive** | Warm, bounding pulses, wide pulse pressure (early), fever or rash |
| **Mixed** | Common, e.g. septic shock with cardiomyopathy |

Warm and cold shock help differentiate, but sepsis can be cold late, and mixed states occur.

## Staging

Compensated (tachycardia, vasoconstriction), decompensated (hypotension), and refractory shock with progressive organ dysfunction. Organ failure alone does not establish irreversibility; reassess reversibility and goals of care. Response to fluid and vasopressor guides therapy; **serial lactate trajectory** contributes to reassessment but is not an exclusive resuscitation goal; capillary refill, output and congestion also matter.

## Self-marking checklist

- Defines shock as an oxygen delivery problem
- Perfusion signs and haemodynamics
- Targeted history
- Investigations including point-of-care ultrasound
- Dynamic assessment
- Classification of types with features
- Staging
- Monitoring response

items.title: 15. Occult bleeding in an older patient on a beta-blocker
items.q: An 82-year-old patient taking a beta-blocker has occult postoperative bleeding. The heart rate is 72/min, BP 110/65 mmHg and initial haemoglobin is unchanged. Explain how you would recognise shock and why these observations may mislead.
items.a:
## Why the observations do not exclude shock

Blood loss reduces venous return/stroke volume before pressure necessarily falls. Sympathetic vasoconstriction and mobilisation of unstressed venous blood may temporarily preserve MAP. In an older patient, baseline hypertension may make 110 systolic a substantial relative reduction; reduced cardiac/renal reserve reduces tolerance of loss. Beta-blockade can suppress tachycardia, and a pacemaker can fix the rate. Initial Hb may remain unchanged when whole blood is lost proportionately, then fall with redistribution or fluid replacement. None of these values measures current oxygen delivery.

## Effect of anaesthesia and medication

Anaesthetic vasodilation/myocardial depression or neuraxial sympathectomy attenuate compensation. Sedatives/opioids obscure altered mentation, pain and respiratory responses. Mechanical ventilation/PEEP reduces venous return and changes the interpretation of CVP and dynamic indices. ACEI/ARB and other vasodilators can magnify hypotension. Conversely, vasopressors can restore BP while leaving inadequate flow. Shock index is also less reliable with beta-blockade/pacing.

## Recognition and action

Review baseline/trends, operation, drains, dressings, abdomen and possible concealed bleeding. Check CRT, mottling, skin temperature, pulse volume/pulse pressure, alertness when assessable, urine and serial lactate/base deficit. Verify all measurements and check airway/circuit if ETCO₂ falls. Obtain serial blood gas/Hb, group/crossmatch, coagulation/fibrinogen and calcium; focused echo may help distinguish underfilling, pump dysfunction and obstruction. A normal lactate or a small hyperdynamic LV cannot exclude every problem or independently mandate fluid.

Escalate immediately to surgery/anaesthesia, control haemorrhage and activate the local major-haemorrhage pathway when warranted. Replace blood appropriately rather than waiting for Hb to cross a threshold in active major bleeding. Titrate perfusion support, keep warm and repeatedly reassess the response. Do not transport an unstable patient for diagnostic imaging when urgent haemostasis is required.

> **Evidence anchor:** Current Set 1 Learn notes §§2–3; ESICM monitoring recommendations (2025). See the source section for review depth and links.

## Self-marking checklist

- Explains compensated shock and pressure versus flow
- Explains age/baseline disease and impaired physiological reserve
- Explains beta-blocker/pacemaker effects on HR/shock index
- Explains anaesthesia, sedation, vasodilators and ventilation effects
- Explains why initial Hb can be normal
- Uses serial perfusion signs, relevant labs and focused imaging
- Prioritises haemostasis/blood resuscitation without waiting for a number

items.title: 16. Distributive shock refractory to noradrenaline
items.q: Describe the pathophysiology of distributive shock and outline your management of a patient with vasodilatory shock refractory to noradrenaline.
items.a:
## Pathophysiology

**Distributive shock** is **pathological vasodilatation** with maldistribution of flow, often with normal or high cardiac output, although low output may coexist. Causes: sepsis, anaphylaxis, neurogenic shock, vasoplegia after cardiopulmonary bypass, adrenal crisis, drugs, pancreatitis and burns.
Mechanisms: **inflammatory mediators** (nitric oxide, prostacyclin) activate vascular smooth muscle K-ATP channels and inducible nitric oxide synthase; **relative vasopressin deficiency**; adrenoceptor downregulation; endothelial leak and capillary hypovolaemia; mitochondrial dysfunction; myocardial depression in sepsis.

## Management

- **1.** **Treat the cause** (immediate antimicrobials, ideally within 1 h for septic shock/probable or definite sepsis; urgent anatomical source control as soon as feasible, ideally within 6 h where required—not a universal 1-h procedural deadline, adrenaline for anaphylaxis, spinal stabilisation for neurogenic).
- **2.** **Fluid:** 2026 SSC conditionally suggests **at least 30 mL/kg crystalloid within the first 3 hours** for sepsis-induced hypoperfusion/shock, with **frequent patient-specific reassessment**; profound unstable shock may justify simultaneous fluid and early peripheral noradrenaline. Beyond the initial phase give further fluid only if need, responsiveness and tolerance justify it.
- **3.** **Noradrenaline** first-line, MAP 65 mmHg; central or peripheral venous access initially.
- **4.** **Ongoing/refractory vasodilatory shock** (escalation depends on trajectory and local practice, **not one absolute noradrenaline-dose cutoff**):
  - Add **vasopressin 0.03 units/min** (reduces noradrenaline need, catecholamine-sparing).
  - Consider **hydrocortisone** for selected ongoing vasopressor-dependent septic shock per local protocol (often 200 mg/day); distinguish sepsis evidence from isolated non-septic vasoplegia.
  - Consider **adrenaline** (if low cardiac output) or **dobutamine** for septic cardiomyopathy.
  - **Methylene blue or angiotensin II** are specialist rescue options in selected severe vasoplegia, not routine steps for every septic patient. Methylene blue examples are **1–2 mg/kg over 15–30 min**; check serotonergic medication/G6PD deficiency, PVR and oximeter interference. Angiotensin II supports MAP but proven survival benefit is lacking; consider thromboembolic risk. Hydroxocobalamin is exceptional off-label rescue with laboratory/dialysis interference. Do not substitute routine vitamin C, beta-blockade or early RRT without an indication for cause-directed treatment.
  - Exclude missed causes (hypovolaemia, tamponade, pneumothorax, adrenal insufficiency, bowel ischaemia), correct hypoxaemia and clinically important electrolyte/metabolic abnormalities; treat endocrine disease when supported by the presentation.
- **5.** **Monitoring**: arterial line, lactate, ScvO2, cardiac output, echocardiography.
- **6.** **Organ support**: ventilation, renal replacement therapy, ICU.

> **Evidence anchor:** Management of vasoplegic shock (2025); current SSC guidance. See the source section for review depth and links.

## Self-marking checklist

- Defines distributive shock and gives causes
- Mechanisms (nitric oxide, vasopressin deficiency, leak)
- First-line noradrenaline and target MAP
- Adjuncts for refractory shock (vasopressin, steroid, methylene blue)
- Reassess for missed causes
- Treats the underlying cause
- Monitoring and organ support
- Fluid strategy

items.title: 17. Cardiogenic shock
items.q: Discuss the causes, diagnosis and management of cardiogenic shock.
items.a:
## Definition and causes

Cardiogenic shock is **inadequate tissue perfusion primarily from cardiac pump failure** despite adequate or elevated filling, sometimes with normotension from compensatory vasoconstriction. A low CI (often ~<2.2 L/min/m²) and elevated PAOP may support LV-predominant shock, but **fixed BP/CI/PCWP thresholds are not diagnostic requirements** (especially for RV-predominant or mixed shock).
**Causes**: acute **myocardial infarction** (most common), acute-on-chronic heart failure, **mechanical** (papillary muscle rupture, ventricular septal rupture, free wall rupture), **valve disease** (acute regurgitation, severe stenosis), myocarditis, arrhythmia, Takotsubo, stress, and drug-induced (beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers).

## Diagnosis

Clinical: cold, clammy, raised JVP, pulmonary oedema, S3, murmur. **ECG** and troponin, **echocardiography** (ventricular function, mechanical complications, tamponade, valves), chest X-ray, lactate and gases, and invasive monitoring (arterial line, pulmonary artery catheter in selected patients). Exclude obstructive causes (PE, tamponade, tension pneumothorax).

## Management

- **ABC** with oxygen; **avoid intubation** unless required (induction can cause collapse); if needed, ketamine or etomidate, vasopressor ready.
- **Reperfusion** (PCI) in MI; surgery for mechanical complications.
- **Haemodynamic support**: **noradrenaline** to MAP 65 (first-line over dopamine, based on SOAP II); **dobutamine** (2 to 20 micrograms/kg/min) or **milrinone** for low output; **levosimendan** in some centres; avoid fluid overload but consider small reassessed boluses **only when genuinely underfilled**; RV infarction is not an automatic indication for fluid loading.
- **Mechanical support:** select with a shock team and an explicit bridge/exit plan. IABP-SHOCK II did not support routine IABP for infarct-related shock, although specific mechanical lesions may differ. **DanGer-Shock (2024)** found lower 180-day mortality with a microaxial pump in selected STEMI-shock patients, with more serious device complications/RRT. **ECLS-SHOCK (2023)** found no 30-day mortality benefit from routine early VA-ECLS and more bleeding/vascular complications. Neither supports automatic device escalation for every shock phenotype.
- Treat arrhythmias, correct acidosis, electrolytes, and consider renal replacement.
- **Shock team** approach, ICU, and goals of care.

## Self-marking checklist

- Defines pump-failure hypoperfusion; explains supportive rather than mandatory pressure/CI thresholds
- Causes including mechanical complications
- Investigations including echocardiography
- Careful airway management
- Reperfusion strategy
- Vasopressor and inotrope choices
- Mechanical circulatory support options
- Multidisciplinary approach

items.title: 18. Mixed shock, low flow and venous congestion
items.q: A postoperative patient has MAP 64 mmHg, high CVP, oliguria, mottled skin and a falling ETCO₂ despite noradrenaline. Discuss how you would distinguish mixed shock, low flow and venous congestion.
items.a:
## Why the pressure is misleading

MAP may have recovered through SVR while **forward CO and effective organ driving pressure remain inadequate**. High CVP may represent RV dysfunction, TR, PEEP, tamponade, intra-abdominal hypertension or fluid accumulation. The kidney depends on both inflow and outflow pressure; a high venous pressure can reduce renal perfusion even with MAP 64.

## Diagnostic priorities

- Check pulse/arterial trace and respiratory circuit; fall in ETCO₂ with controlled ventilation can signal **falling pulmonary blood flow**, but also ventilation/dead-space or sampling changes.
- Assess surgical site/drains for occult bleeding, infection/source control, drugs, rhythm/ECG, airway pressure and PEEP.
- Focused TTE/TOE to examine LV/RV function, pericardial collection, RV pressure/volume load, valve disease, LVOTO, lung B-lines and vena cava. If available, measure CO/SV trend and consider venous Doppler congestion markers in context.
- Use Hb, gas/base deficit, lactate trend, kidney function and ScvO₂ ± CO₂ gap as adjuncts, recognising each can mislead in isolation.

## Management by mechanism

- **Bleeding:** surgical haemostasis and appropriate blood replacement.
- **Vasoplegia:** adequate but not excessive vasopressor to achieve perfusion pressure (noradrenaline ± vasopressin) while reassessing output.
- **Low CO:** treat rhythm/ischaemia and consider selected inotropy if low-flow pump failure is established; avoid escalating afterload without considering SV.
- **Obstruction:** decompress tamponade/tension process and correct high intra-abdominal pressure where appropriate.
- **Venous congestion:** avoid reflex fluid boluses; optimise RV afterload, PEEP and volume; consider decongestion once safe.

## Endpoints

Trend peripheral perfusion, mentation, urine, ETCO₂, CO/SV, lactate, renal function and absence of worsening overload. Reassess diagnosis after each treatment.

## Self-marking checklist

- Recognises MAP is not CO and high CVP may reduce organ driving pressure
- Checks bleeding, devices, ventilator and causes of changing ETCO₂
- Uses focused ultrasound to discriminate RV/LV failure, obstruction and volume status
- Interprets labs and venous signals in context, not as single-fluid triggers
- Treats bleeding/vasoplegia/low output/obstruction by mechanism
- Avoids automatic fluid boluses in congested patients
- Specifies objective serial perfusion and congestion endpoints

items.title: 19. Neurogenic shock in cervical spinal cord injury
items.q: Discuss the cardiovascular management of a patient with a cervical spinal cord injury and neurogenic shock requiring surgery.
items.a:
## Pathophysiology

Injury above T6 interrupts descending sympathetic outflow: **vasodilatation (low SVR)**, **bradycardia** (unopposed vagal tone, T1–T4 cardiac accelerators lost), reduced venous return, hypotension, hypothermia (poikilothermia). It differs from **spinal shock** (loss of reflexes and tone) and from haemorrhagic shock (which must be excluded in trauma).

## Management

- **Resuscitation**: ABC with **cervical spine precautions**, oxygen, and a search for other injuries (haemorrhage can coexist, with tachycardia absent).
- **Targets:** the 2024 acute traumatic SCI guideline **weakly suggests MAP augmentation to at least 75–80 mmHg without actively targeting beyond 90–95 mmHg for 3–7 days** (very low certainty); individualise and avoid hypoxaemia/hypotension. Do not apply this to all neurogenic-shock contexts.
- **Fluids**: restore euvolaemia without overload (pulmonary oedema is common due to neurogenic changes).
- **Vasopressors:** noradrenaline is often selected to support vascular tone and cardiac output; individualise. Pure alpha stimulation can worsen bradycardia and dopamine has arrhythmia risks. The SCI guideline did not establish one superior agent. Treat significant bradycardia with atropine, appropriate adrenaline support or pacing as required.
- **Anaesthesia**: intubation with in-line stabilisation (avoid suxamethonium after 48 hours because of hyperkalaemia), expect **profound hypotension and bradycardia with laryngoscopy and suction**, arterial line, ventilate carefully; **autonomic dysreflexia** is a risk in chronic injuries above T6.
- **Temperature**, DVT prophylaxis, pressure care, and stress ulcer prophylaxis.
- **Respiratory** support and early ICU.

## Self-marking checklist

- Mechanism of neurogenic shock
- Distinguish from spinal shock and haemorrhage
- Blood pressure targets
- Vasopressor and bradycardia treatment
- Airway and suxamethonium caution
- Anticipation of vagal responses
- Temperature and pressure care
- ICU care

items.title: 20. Tamponade after cardiac surgery
items.q: A 45-year-old man becomes hypotensive and tachycardic after cardiac surgery. Discuss the diagnosis and management of cardiac tamponade.
items.a:
## Pathophysiology

Fluid or blood in the pericardium raises intrapericardial pressure, limiting diastolic filling, reducing stroke volume and cardiac output (obstructive shock). **Rate of accumulation** matters more than volume: acute accumulation of 100 to 200 mL can be fatal, whereas slow effusions of 1 litre may be tolerated. Causes: post-cardiac surgery, trauma, aortic dissection, malignancy, uraemia, infection, anticoagulation, and iatrogenic (central line, pacemaker).

## Diagnosis

- **Beck's triad**: hypotension, raised JVP, muffled heart sounds (not always present).
- **Pulsus paradoxus** (fall in systolic BP over 10 mmHg on inspiration), tachycardia, narrow pulse pressure, oliguria; after cardiac surgery, **sudden fall in chest drain output** with rising CVP and equalisation of pressures.
- **ECG**: low voltage, electrical alternans. **CXR**: widened cardiac silhouette.
- **Echo**: effusion and haemodynamic evidence (RA collapse, RV diastolic collapse where present, IVC congestion, altered respiratory inflow). **Positive-pressure ventilation, high RA pressure and loculated postoperative clot can mask classic signs**, and a small effusion can still cause important tamponade.

## Management

- **1.** **Call surgeon/cardiologist.** Oxygen.
