- **2.** Protect systemic perfusion while arranging **definitive decompression**. Small assessed fluid may bridge clear underfilling but **avoid repeated indiscriminate boluses**. Maintain compensatory rate and avoid hypotension or marked vasodilation; titrate vasoactive support to physiology.
- **3.** **Induction** (if needed): coordinate with the procedural/surgical team with immediate decompression available; preserve spontaneous ventilation when feasible, avoid abrupt vasodilation or high PEEP, and have blood/vasopressor support ready. Choose drugs and doses to minimise cardiovascular collapse.
- **4.** **Definitive drainage in this postoperative patient:** urgent **surgical re-exploration** for suspected loculated clot or ongoing bleeding; TOE is useful when TTE is nondiagnostic but must not delay treatment in collapse. Image-guided pericardiocentesis can suit selected accessible non-clotted effusions. If arrest occurs, follow the cardiac-surgery arrest protocol with immediate surgical involvement and rapid resternotomy where indicated.
- **5.** **After drainage**: monitor for recurrence and reperfusion, treat the cause.

> **Evidence anchor:** Pericardial effusions and tamponade (2020). See the source section for review depth and links.

## Self-marking checklist

- Pathophysiology and importance of rate of accumulation
- Clinical signs (Beck's triad, pulsus paradoxus)
- Post-cardiac surgery clues
- Echo findings
- Preload and chronotropy support
- Anaesthetic principles (avoid positive pressure, vasodilators)
- Pericardiocentesis versus surgical drainage
- Follow-up

items.title: 21. Stressed volume, Pmsf and noradrenaline
items.q: Explain stressed venous volume and mean systemic filling pressure. How can noradrenaline improve venous return without giving more fluid, and why might cardiac output nevertheless fall?
items.a:
## The venous reservoir and return gradient

Unstressed volume fills the vascular space without generating appreciable recoil pressure; stressed volume stretches vessels and generates pressure. These are functional concepts that change with venous tone, not two anatomically separate tanks. **Mean systemic filling pressure (Pmsf)** describes the equilibrium pressure in the systemic circulation at zero flow. In a simplified model, **venous return = (Pmsf − right atrial pressure)/resistance to venous return**. At steady state venous return equals CO.

## Vasodilation and hypovolaemia

Venodilation increases capacitance and shifts volume towards the unstressed compartment, potentially lowering Pmsf/venous return without a fall in total blood volume. Actual haemorrhage reduces available volume. These can coexist. Raising CVP alone does not establish improved filling or flow; it can indicate failing RV ejection or increased intrathoracic pressure.

## Effects of noradrenaline

Venoconstriction, especially of capacitance beds, can recruit unstressed volume and increase Pmsf/preload. Arterial vasoconstriction restores perfusion pressure, while modest beta-1 effects and improved coronary pressure may support contraction. If the ventricle is preload responsive and able to eject, CO may increase without an additional fluid bolus.

The response is not guaranteed. Increased LV afterload may reduce SV in a poorly contracting heart; increased resistance to venous return, RV dysfunction, excessive vasoconstriction or an increased RAP may limit benefit. In LVOTO, catecholamine inotropy can be counterproductive. A higher MAP therefore does not establish better tissue flow.

## Bedside application

Choose fluid, a vasopressor, inotropy or obstruction relief according to the mechanism. Evaluate perfusion and measured CO/SV response where indicated, plus lung/venous congestion. Do not use Pmsf as a routine bedside number to chase, and do not interpret a higher CVP after noradrenaline as proof of improved circulating volume.

> **Evidence anchor:** Vasoactive therapy in shock (2021); Management of vasoplegic shock (2025). See the source section for review depth and links.

## Self-marking checklist

- Defines stressed versus unstressed volume without treating them as separate anatomical tanks
- Defines Pmsf and the venous-return gradient/resistance relationship
- Distinguishes absolute loss from venodilation/relative underfilling
- Explains noradrenaline's venous recruitment, arterial and cardiac effects
- Explains why afterload/RV dysfunction can prevent CO improvement
- Uses perfusion/flow response and congestion rather than MAP/CVP alone

items.title: 22. Predicting fluid responsiveness in a ventilated patient
items.q: Discuss the methods of predicting fluid responsiveness in a ventilated patient and the role of goal-directed fluid therapy.
items.a:
## Concept

Fluid responsiveness is often operationalised as an **~10–15% rise in SV/CO** after a preload change; the exact proportion of patients responsive varies by cohort. **Responsiveness is not the same as clinical need or safety of further fluid**. Static pressures (CVP, PAOP) predict poorly; dynamic tests use heart–lung interactions or reversible preload transfer.

## Methods

- **PPV/SVV:** around 12–13% may support responsiveness **under valid conditions** (controlled ventilation, regular rhythm, adequate respiratory mechanics/tidal volume, closed chest). Low VT, AF, RV dysfunction and raised intra-abdominal pressure limit utility; a fixed 8 mL/kg VT is **not a requirement to ventilate unsafely**, and a tidal-volume challenge can sometimes clarify.
- **Passive leg raising** with cardiac output measurement (a rise over 10%): works in spontaneous breathing and arrhythmia; reversible "autotransfusion".
- **End-expiratory occlusion test** and **tidal volume challenge**.
- **Echocardiography**: measure LVOT VTI change during a valid preload challenge. IVC variation has major confounders; **LV end-diastolic area alone is a static measurement**, not a reliable responsiveness test.
- **Mini-fluid challenge** (100 to 250 mL over 1 to 2 minutes) with a cardiac output monitor.

## Goal-directed fluid therapy

Selects a physiological objective (perfusion, SV/CO, oxygen delivery), tests a targeted intervention and measures response **and signs of congestion**. Avoid automatic repeated boluses merely to maximise SV; stop or redirect treatment when perfusion does not improve or fluid becomes unsafe. Oesophageal Doppler, pulse contour and echocardiography are tools, not prescriptions.
- **Evidence**: benefit in high-risk major abdominal surgery in meta-analyses (fewer complications), but **OPTIMISE** showed no significant reduction in complications, and **OPTIMISE II** no benefit; the benefit of routine protocolised use remains uncertain in contemporary care. In OPTIMISE II the tested bundle did not reduce infections and increased early cardiac events; targeted monitoring in an unstable high-risk individual remains a separate clinical decision.
- **Avoid overload** (oedema, anastomotic leak), and avoid hypovolaemia (AKI).

> **Evidence anchor:** ESICM monitoring recommendations (2025); OPTIMISE II (2024). See the source section for review depth and links.

## Self-marking checklist

- Defines responsiveness using SV/CO change; separates response, need and tolerance
- Weakness of CVP
- PPV/SVV with conditions of validity
- Passive leg raise
- Echo-based methods
- Goal-directed protocol and evidence
- Complications of overload and hypovolaemia
- Role in ERAS

items.title: 23. Septic shock with B-lines and a rising CVP: more fluid?
items.q: A patient recovering from septic shock has MAP 67 mmHg, improving capillary refill and mentation, lactate 5.8 mmol/L, bilateral B-lines and a rising CVP. Is more fluid indicated? Explain your reasoning.
items.a:
## Interpretation

There is **no automatic indication for more fluid**. Improving CRT/mentation are positive signs; high lactate may reflect ongoing shock, catecholamine stimulation, delayed clearance or another process. B-lines and a rising CVP suggest **fluid intolerance/venous congestion** (not proof of excess circulating volume). A MAP of 67 cannot establish adequate cardiac output.

## Reassessment

- Recheck trend in vital signs, skin perfusion, urine, renal/liver status, lactate and base deficit; review source control, antimicrobial timing and vasoactive/adrenergic exposure.
- Use focused echo for LV/RV size/function, filling, B-lines, tamponade and signs of venous congestion; consider CO/SV monitoring when response is unclear.
- Ask separately **need**, **responsiveness** and **tolerance**. If considering more fluid, use a **reversible PLR with measured LVOT VTI/CO**, not a static CVP/IVC value alone.
- Consider a veno-arterial CO₂ gap/ScvO₂ as **adjuncts** where already available; each is confounded.

## Management

- Avoid further indiscriminate boluses. Treat an ongoing source, correct reversible problems, and optimise noradrenaline/vasopressin in **vasoplegia** or use an appropriately selected inotrope if **true low output** remains after evaluation.
- If congested and perfusion stable, limit new fluid and consider **deresuscitation** when appropriate; if the patient is genuinely underfilled with measurable benefit and tolerance, a small monitored challenge may be reasonable.
- Reassess objectively after each intervention; do **not** aim to normalise lactate by fluid alone.

> **Evidence anchor:** Fluids in sepsis (2026); ESICM monitoring recommendations (2025). See the source section for review depth and links.

## Self-marking checklist

- Does not reflexively prescribe fluid for lactate 5.8 or MAP 67
- Distinguishes lactate production/clearance from contemporaneous tissue perfusion
- Explains need–responsiveness–tolerance and B-lines/CVP caveats
- Uses focused echo and, where relevant, PLR with measured CO/VTI
- Reassesses source control, myocardial output and vasoplegia
- Makes a cause-specific plan while avoiding congestion
- Defines serial outcome measures and a stop rule

items.title: 24. Fluid de-escalation after septic shock
items.q: After resuscitation for septic shock, a patient is 6 L fluid-positive with peripheral oedema, worsening oxygenation and stable perfusion on a falling noradrenaline dose. Discuss fluid de-escalation and deresuscitation.
items.a:
## Assess readiness and the cause of fluid accumulation

Confirm source control and improving shock. Review MAP/CO where indicated, CRT, lactate trajectory, mentation, urine, renal function, electrolytes and vasoactive trend. Examine lung and venous congestion; cumulative balance and weight trends help but charting can be inaccurate. Oedema may coexist with intravascular underfilling. Exclude ARDS, cardiac failure and new infection as causes of deteriorating oxygenation.

## De-escalation — stop avoidable intake

Stop unnecessary resuscitation/maintenance fluid. Count **drug carriers, flushes, nutrition and oral/enteral intake**. Concentrate infusions where safe, prescribe necessary electrolyte/nutritional support, and separately replace measured abnormal losses. Do not stop essential therapy simply to achieve a balance target.

## Active removal — only when appropriate

If excess fluid is impairing organ function and perfusion is sufficiently stable, consider a monitored loop-diuretic trial, individualised to renal function and prior exposure. A small, falling vasopressor requirement is not an absolute bar, but worsening shock is a reason to stop/reassess. Set a patient-specific net balance/weight and oxygenation goal; no universal litres-per-day target is established.

Use renal replacement therapy for standard indications, including clinically important refractory fluid overload when appropriate; do not institute routine extracorporeal removal solely because a numerical positive balance exists. Evidence for outcome benefit from a universal deresuscitation protocol remains incomplete.

## Monitor and stop rules

Follow BP/perfusion, pressor requirement, urine, weight/balance, oxygenation, creatinine, Na/K/Mg and acid–base. Stop or slow removal if hypotension, increasing pressor need, worsening perfusion, important electrolyte disturbance or other intolerance develops. Reassess the fluid prescription daily as physiology changes.

> **Evidence anchor:** Fluids in sepsis (2026). See the source section for review depth and links.

## Self-marking checklist

- Assesses shock recovery and competing causes of oedema/hypoxaemia
- Distinguishes excess total fluid from intravascular filling
- Counts hidden fluid inputs and stops avoidable intake
- Uses individualised diuresis only when benefit and tolerance justify it
- Explains selective RRT rather than routine ultrafiltration
- Defines serial monitoring and stop rules
- Acknowledges uncertainty about outcome benefit and universal targets

items.title: 25. Pharmacology of noradrenaline, adrenaline, vasopressin and dobutamine
items.q: Compare the pharmacology and clinical use of noradrenaline, adrenaline, vasopressin and dobutamine in the management of shock.
items.a:
| Drug | Receptors and effects | Use | Dose and cautions |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Noradrenaline** | Alpha-1 (strong), beta-1 (moderate); raises SVR and MAP, modest rise in CO | **First-line** for septic and most distributive shock; cardiogenic shock with hypotension | 0.01 to 0.5 micrograms/kg/min; central access preferred; ischaemia, arrhythmia |
| **Adrenaline** | Beta-1, beta-2, alpha-1 (dose-dependent): rises CO, SVR at high dose | Anaphylaxis, cardiac arrest, cardiogenic shock, refractory septic shock | 0.01 to 0.5 micrograms/kg/min; lactic acidosis (beta-2), hyperglycaemia, arrhythmia, splanchnic ischaemia |
| **Vasopressin** | V1 receptors in vascular smooth muscle (no catecholamine effect); V2 renal | Add-on in septic shock and vasoplegia; catecholamine-sparing | Fixed 0.03 to 0.04 units/min; digital, mesenteric, and coronary ischaemia, hyponatraemia |
| **Dobutamine** | Beta-1 (and beta-2); inotropy, chronotropy, vasodilatation | Low cardiac output with adequate MAP, septic cardiomyopathy, cardiogenic shock | 2 to 20 micrograms/kg/min; arrhythmia, hypotension from vasodilatation, tolerance |

## Principles

Dose ranges above are examples, not universal ceilings. Check concentration, infusion-pump settings, line patency, formulation conventions and the local high-risk medication policy.

- Aim for an **individualised target MAP (often initially 65 mmHg in septic shock)** and perfusion markers (lactate, urine output, capillary refill), not a drug.
- **Combine** agents with differing mechanisms to limit toxicity.
- **Evidence:** SOAP II found **more arrhythmias** with dopamine and a concerning cardiogenic-shock subgroup mortality signal, **not a significant overall mortality difference**; VASST found no overall mortality benefit with adjunctive vasopressin; CATS found no mortality difference between adrenaline and noradrenaline plus dobutamine.
- Treat reversible hypovolaemia, hypoxaemia and important metabolic/electrolyte abnormalities **concurrently**; do not delay vasopressors in profound vasodilatory shock until these are fully corrected.

> **Evidence anchor:** Vasoactive therapy in shock (2021); Management of vasoplegic shock (2025). See the source section for review depth and links.

## Self-marking checklist

- Receptor pharmacology of each drug
- First-line choice and indication
- Doses and routes
- Adverse effects
- Rationale for combination
- Key trials (SOAP II, VASST)
- Targets
- Correct reversible factors

items.title: 26. Milrinone and levosimendan in low cardiac output
items.q: Describe the pharmacology and role of milrinone and levosimendan in a patient with low cardiac output.
items.a:
## Milrinone

- **Phosphodiesterase-3 inhibitor** raising cAMP independently of beta-receptors: **inotropy, lusitropy, and vasodilatation** (systemic and pulmonary).
- **Dose**: loading 25 to 50 micrograms/kg over 10 minutes (often omitted to avoid hypotension), infusion 0.25 to 0.75 micrograms/kg/min. Half-life **2 to 3 hours**, longer in renal impairment (renally cleared), so reduce the dose.
- **Uses**: low cardiac output after cardiac surgery, right ventricular failure with pulmonary hypertension, and patients on beta-blockers or with beta-receptor downregulation.
- **Adverse effects**: **hypotension** (needs noradrenaline or vasopressin), arrhythmia, thrombocytopenia.

## Levosimendan

- **Calcium sensitiser** (binds troponin C) with **opening of K-ATP channels** (vasodilatation) and PDE-III inhibition; may enhance contraction with less intracellular calcium loading than catecholamines, but this does not guarantee unchanged myocardial oxygen demand or improved outcomes.
- Active metabolite OR-1896 gives prolonged effects for **days** after a 24-hour infusion (commonly 0.05–0.2 micrograms/kg/min); avoid a loading bolus in hypotension and follow local specialist policy.
- **Use**: acute decompensated heart failure, cardiac surgery, weaning from support.
- **Evidence:** LEVO-CTS/LICORN did not establish routine cardiac-surgery benefit. **LeoPARDS** did not reduce organ dysfunction in sepsis and produced more supraventricular tachyarrhythmia; it is not routine septic-shock organ protection. Availability varies.
- **Adverse effects**: hypotension, arrhythmia (AF), headache.

## Comparison

Both are inodilators that work despite beta-blockade, and both can cause hypotension. Milrinone has a shorter duration than levosimendan but a **2–3-hour half-life**, so it is not rapidly reversible and accumulates in renal impairment; levosimendan has a long duration.

> **Evidence anchor:** Vasoactive therapy in shock (2021); Novel therapies in sepsis (2025), selected sections. See the source section for review depth and links.

## Self-marking checklist

- Mechanism of each drug
- Haemodynamic effects
- Doses and half-life
- Renal adjustment for milrinone
- Indications
- Adverse effects
- Evidence for levosimendan
- Comparison and practical use

items.title: 27. Dynamic LVOT obstruction after escalating dobutamine
items.q: A shocked patient develops a hyperdynamic left ventricle, systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve and a late-peaking LVOT Doppler signal after escalating dobutamine. Discuss diagnosis and management.
items.a:
## Interpretation

This suggests **dynamic LV outflow tract obstruction (LVOTO)**, sometimes with SAM-related mitral regurgitation. Low preload/afterload, tachycardia and catecholamine-driven contractility can produce obstruction even without known HCM. A high EF does not establish adequate forward stroke volume. Increasing inotropy can worsen hypotension.

## Assessment

Confirm the arterial reading, rhythm, preload/afterload changes, bleeding and drug doses. Use expert TTE/TOE to confirm the obstructive Doppler pattern and SAM, assess MR and RV function, and exclude fixed AS, global pump failure and tamponade. Interpret Doppler in context; avoid confusing an MR jet with LVOT velocity.

## Treatment

- Reduce/stop provoking dobutamine and avoid reflex escalation of adrenaline. Treat pain, fever, arrhythmia and other tachycardia drivers.
- Restore vascular tone with a **non-inotropic vasoconstrictor**, commonly phenylephrine or vasopressin, titrated to perfusion. Noradrenaline is useful in vasoplegia but its beta effect can aggravate obstruction in some patients.
- Correct demonstrable underfilling with a small monitored isotonic bolus only if tolerated; SAM-associated MR/pulmonary oedema limits fluid safety.
- In selected patients, expert-guided titration of a short-acting beta-blocker can reduce obstruction after pressure support and confirmation of physiology; it is not empirical treatment for undifferentiated shock.
- Reassess LVOT gradient, forward SV/VTI, MR, perfusion and congestion. Arrange ICU/cardiology review and follow-up for underlying HCM if relevant.

> **Evidence anchor:** ACC/AHA perioperative HCM/LVOTO recommendations (2024). See the source section for review depth and links.

## Self-marking checklist

- Recognises dynamic LVOTO/SAM and distinguishes high EF from adequate forward flow
- Identifies preload, afterload, HR and inotropy triggers
- Uses echo/Doppler with attention to differential diagnosis and MR
- Reduces provoking inotropy rather than escalating it
- Restores afterload and cautiously treats genuine underfilling
- Restricts beta-blockade to confirmed physiology with appropriate support/expertise
- Defines reassessment and follow-up

items.title: 28. Emergency pericardiocentesis
items.q: Describe how you would perform an emergency pericardiocentesis.
items.a:
## Indications and preparation

Haemodynamically significant tamponade with an accessible fluid collection, especially medical effusion. Surgery is preferred for clotted postoperative/traumatic blood, an active surgical lesion or unsuitable percutaneous access; image-guided drainage is not restricted solely to settings without surgery. Call for help, give oxygen, secure IV access, **resuscitation drugs** and a defibrillator ready, sterile technique, local anaesthetic, and sedate only minimally. Use **ultrasound** to locate the largest pocket of fluid closest to the skin, and mark depth.

## Technique (real-time ultrasound-guided, using the safest window)

- **1.** **Choose the safest pocket:** map the effusion with echo and select the shortest accessible route that avoids myocardium, vessels, lung and liver; this may be apical, parasternal or subxiphoid. Position/consent when feasible without compromising perfusion.
- **2.** Full monitoring, IV access, asepsis, local anaesthetic, resuscitation equipment and surgical backup; review anticoagulation without delaying life-saving drainage.
- **3.** Advance the needle with **real-time ultrasound needle-tip visualisation** where feasible, aspirating with care and maintaining awareness of depth and trajectory; historical subxiphoid landmarks do not replace imaging.
- **4.** **Confirm intrapericardial access** by needle-tip imaging and aspiration; agitated-saline contrast on echo can help when uncertain. **Blood aspiration alone does not prove pericardial position.**
- **5.** Pass the guidewire and place a pigtail catheter by a controlled Seldinger technique; drain enough promptly to restore perfusion and reassess echo/BP.
- **6.** Continue monitored drainage according to physiology and the cause. For a large **chronic** effusion, avoid unnecessary rapid complete evacuation (pericardial decompression syndrome); leave a catheter and reassess recurrence. No fixed initial aspirate or catheter duration applies to every patient.

**Exception:** penetrating trauma and clotted postcardiac-surgical haemopericardium usually demand **surgical relief and haemostasis** rather than relying on a needle.

## Complications

**Myocardial or coronary laceration**, arrhythmia, pneumothorax, liver puncture, infection, and failure when the blood is clotted (traumatic and post-surgical tamponade need surgery).

## After the procedure

Chest X-ray, repeat echocardiography, and send fluid for analysis.

> **Evidence anchor:** Pericardial effusions and tamponade (2020). See the source section for review depth and links.

## Self-marking checklist

- Indication and preparation
- Ultrasound guidance
- Image-selected safest access route; no mandatory subxiphoid direction
- Confirmation of position
- Drain placement by Seldinger
- Physiological drainage endpoint, follow-up monitoring and decompression-syndrome precaution
- Complications
- Limitations in clotted blood

items.title: 29. Penetrating chest trauma with haemopericardium
items.q: A patient with penetrating chest trauma becomes hypotensive with a rapidly expanding haemopericardium on focused ultrasound. Describe the resuscitation, anaesthetic approach and definitive management.
items.a:
## Mechanism

Rapid blood accumulation raises pericardial pressure, preventing diastolic filling, reducing SV/CO and causing **obstructive shock**. The causative cardiac injury may be **actively bleeding**; blood may clot and prevent percutaneous drainage. A negative or equivocal ultrasound does not fully exclude cardiac injury when the clinical suspicion is high.

## Immediate management

- Activate trauma, cardiac/thoracic surgical, anaesthetic and blood-bank help. Prioritise **urgent haemorrhage control and surgical relief of tamponade** while providing oxygen and appropriate life support.
- Large-bore IV/IO access, rapid blood-product availability, warming, calcium/coagulation monitoring and major haemorrhage protocol where indicated.
- Coordinate whether to preserve spontaneous ventilation until surgical decompression; induction and positive-pressure ventilation may precipitate arrest. Prepare an appropriate haemodynamically conservative induction and immediately available procedural team; do not delay definitive treatment in pursuit of an ideal blood pressure.
- Assess associated tension pneumothorax/haemothorax and decompress chest when indicated. Do not waste time on CT in an unstable patient with a surgical lesion.

## Definitive therapy and exceptions

- **Emergency thoracotomy/sternotomy, evacuation of blood and cardiac repair** is the appropriate definitive approach when feasible; resuscitative thoracotomy depends on arrest/peri-arrest status, injury and local trauma protocol.
- Needle pericardiocentesis may only provide temporary relief when surgical decompression is **unavailable or delayed** and may fail because of clot or ongoing bleeding; it cannot repair a cardiac wound.
- Continue haemostatic and organ-perfusion resuscitation after decompression, watching for rebleeding and myocardial dysfunction.

> **Evidence anchor:** Pericardial effusions and tamponade (2020); Set 1 trauma teaching. See the source section for review depth and links.

## Self-marking checklist

- Explains acute pressure-volume physiology and possible active cardiac bleeding
- Calls trauma/cardiac surgery and prepares immediate surgical decompression
- Provides haemostatic resuscitation and source control rather than repeated crystalloid
- Plans induction/ventilation around high arrest risk
- Distinguishes surgical repair from temporary needle drainage
- Avoids delays for CT in an unstable patient and considers chest injuries
- Plans postoperative monitoring for rebleeding and organ dysfunction

items.title: 2016.1 Q14: Hypertension in PACU after sleeve gastrectomy
items.q: An obese 55-year-old female has undergone sleeve gastrectomy which concluded one hour earlier. The post anaesthetic care unit has called to report a blood pressure of 190/110 mmHg. Discuss your approach to the evaluation and management of the hypertension.
items.model:
> **Examiner alignment:** original report checked. A passing answer needed a reasonable differential with at least three plausible causes, treatment of common causes and a chosen drug regimen. The task is postoperative hypertension, not a general essay about essential hypertension.

## Evaluate urgency and confirm the reading

Attend promptly. Check ABC, alertness, ventilation, SpO₂, HR/rhythm and the BP trend against the preoperative baseline. Repeat with an appropriately sized cuff—particularly important in obesity—or verify the arterial trace. Look for chest pain/ECG ischaemia, pulmonary oedema, neurological change, surgical bleeding and other acute hypertension-mediated organ injury. A single 190/110 reading without injury is not itself a hypertensive emergency.

## Differential in this patient

Common causes include pain, anxiety/agitation, hypoxaemia or hypercapnia (OSA, airway obstruction, opioid-related hypoventilation), nausea, shivering/hypothermia and urinary retention. Review missed antihypertensives/withdrawal, drugs or residual stimulation, fluid excess and chronic uncontrolled BP. Consider less common causes only when supported by the presentation; neurological deterioration may require urgent brain imaging. Examine the abdomen, wounds and drains, and consider surgical complications rather than assuming all agitation is pain.

## Treat the cause and titrate BP treatment

Correct airway obstruction/ventilation, give appropriate oxygen and monitored analgesia without worsening sedation, treat nausea/shivering and relieve retention. If hypertension remains sustained and clinically important, use a short-acting titratable agent selected for physiology. For a tachycardic patient without bronchospasm, bradycardia/heart block or low-output failure, a **labetalol 5–10 mg IV starting bolus**, reassessed and repeated per local policy, is a reasonable perioperative example. A titrated nicardipine infusion is an alternative; nitrates suit myocardial ischaemia or hypertensive pulmonary oedema when not contraindicated.

Avoid an abrupt fall to an arbitrary normal value. With a true hypertensive emergency use monitored, organ-specific treatment; many presentations use an initial MAP reduction no greater than about 20–25% in the first hour, but aortic, obstetric and neurological conditions have different pathways. Escalate to senior anaesthesia/ICU if organ injury, refractory BP or respiratory support is required.

## Follow-up

Repeat BP/perfusion/ventilation assessments after every intervention. Plan recovery disposition, appropriate chronic-drug restart and handover/GP follow-up for persistent hypertension.

items.title: 2015.1 Q4: Septic shock: resuscitation goals and ongoing fluid options
items.q: A 40-year-old 100 kg patient presents with septicaemia of unknown cause. After receiving two litres of 0.9% NaCl (Normal Saline) as initial resuscitation the patient has the following observations: HR 126 bpm; BP 80/40 mmHg. Outline your initial resuscitation goals. (30%) Evaluate options for ongoing fluid resuscitation at this time. (70%)
items.model:
> **Examiner alignment:** original report checked. State at least three goals, then evaluate crystalloids versus colloids rather than spending the whole answer on a sepsis bundle. **Ownership in this revision: Set 1 (fluid-choice emphasis); Set 4 should cross-reference this stem.** Contemporary guidance qualifies the historical answer.

## Resuscitation goals (30%)

Restore effective circulation and tissue perfusion while identifying/treating the infection. Initial goals include an individualised MAP (commonly **65 mmHg** initially), improving CRT/mentation, adequate oxygenation and serial improvement in lactate/base deficit; urine output around **0.5 mL/kg/h** is a contextual, delayed endpoint. Assess cardiac output and congestion when the response is unclear. Do not force every endpoint to normal with fluid alone. Obtain cultures without delaying antimicrobials and arrange prompt source assessment/control.

## Evaluate further fluid (70%)

The observed BP implies MAP about 53 mmHg and serious instability. Confirm the signal, assess perfusion, losses, cardiac function and pulmonary/venous congestion; treat while assessing. The 2 L already given is **20 mL/kg using the stated 100 kg**, but weight alone does not establish obesity or an appropriate final volume. The 2026 SSC suggests ≥30 mL/kg initial crystalloid within 3 h with frequent individualised reassessment; this is not an instruction to give the next litre without considering benefit/tolerance. In unstable shock, start **noradrenaline concurrently** through suitable monitored peripheral access while arranging definitive access if indicated.

- **Balanced isotonic crystalloid:** reasonable default for further resuscitation. Give a monitored aliquot (e.g. 250–500 mL, smaller with limited reserve), reassess forward SV/CO where feasible, CRT/MAP and congestion, and repeat only while beneficial. It reduces chloride exposure compared with further saline, although large trials do not establish a universal mortality advantage.
- **0.9% saline:** available and effective for extracellular-volume replacement, but additional large volumes increase chloride load/hyperchloraemic acidosis. It remains useful in specific settings such as chloride depletion or TBI; neither is described here.
- **Albumin:** potentially less administered volume, but capillary leak reduces retention; expense, overload and lack of an overall survival benefit matter. SAFE/ALBIOS do not justify routine superiority. Selected supplemental use after large crystalloid volumes/cirrhosis differs from routine first-line use; avoid in TBI.
- **HES/gelatin:** avoid HES in sepsis because of renal and outcome harms. Gelatin has uncertain benefit with anaphylaxis/coagulation concerns and is discouraged by current SSC guidance.
- **Blood:** appropriate for significant haemorrhage or a specific transfusion indication, not routine volume expansion in non-bleeding sepsis. Do not pursue a high Hb solely to satisfy historical EGDT.

Use a valid dynamic test when deciding ongoing fluid, and separate **need, responsiveness and tolerance**. If flow/perfusion fail to improve, reconsider vasoplegia, myocardial dysfunction, obstruction or an uncontrolled source. Stop fluid if ineffective or harmful; write maintenance/loss replacement separately.
rubric: States at least three perfusion/resuscitation goals and avoids a single-target approach
Recognises profound instability and calculates prior fluid exposure correctly
Applies initial fluid guidance with reassessment and early concurrent pressors when needed

Allocates answer depth approximately 30% goals and 70% fluid evaluation

items.title: 2015.1 Q3: Pericardial effusion six weeks after cardiac surgery
items.q: A patient who is 6 weeks post cardiac surgery has a pericardial effusion requiring treatment. Outline the symptoms and signs of this condition. (70%) Which of these features would trigger an urgent intervention? (30%)
items.model:
> **Examiner alignment:** original report checked. Show the range from an asymptomatic/slowly developing effusion to acute severe tamponade. **Do not assume that every effusion is tamponade.** Set 1 owns this postoperative effusion stem in this revision; oncology-related effusions remain a different application in Set 18.

## Symptoms and signs (70%)

A slow-growing effusion may be asymptomatic; symptoms depend on rate of accumulation and haemodynamic effect, not simply size. Ask about progressive dyspnoea, reduced exercise tolerance, orthopnoea, fatigue, chest discomfort, dizziness/presyncope and reduced urine. An inflammatory post-pericardiotomy syndrome may include pleuritic pain or fever; anticoagulation/bleeding are relevant to delayed haemopericardium.

Look for tachycardia, raised JVP, narrow pulse pressure, hypotension, pulsus paradoxus (>10 mmHg inspiratory fall in systolic BP during spontaneous breathing), cool peripheries, delayed CRT, altered mentation and oliguria. Heart sounds can be muffled, but **Beck's triad is insensitive**; JVP may not be high with coexisting hypovolaemia. A pericardial rub suggests inflammation rather than establishing tamponade.

Investigations support recognition: ECG may show low voltage/electrical alternans; CXR may show an enlarged globular silhouette in a sufficiently large/chronic effusion but can be normal. **Echo** assesses size, distribution and haemodynamic effect—RA collapse during ventricular systole, RV collapse in early diastole, a plethoric IVC and respiratory filling changes may support tamponade. Loculated postoperative collections, high right-heart pressures and positive-pressure ventilation can obscure classic signs. Use TOE or expert imaging if TTE is inadequate; do not delay decompression in cardiovascular collapse.

## Features requiring urgent action (30%)

Haemodynamic instability or deteriorating organ perfusion consistent with tamponade requires **urgent drainage/surgical review**: progressive hypotension, rising pressor need, syncope/altered mentation, worsening oliguria, marked tachycardia or peri-arrest/arrest. Rapid progression and convincing echo evidence of chamber compression strengthen urgency. Severe breathlessness/orthopnoea, ongoing bleeding or rapidly accumulating effusion also demand immediate specialist assessment.

A stable effusion without haemodynamic compromise does not automatically require emergency drainage just because it is large. In the unstable postoperative patient, loculated clot/ongoing bleeding often favours surgery; accessible non-clotted fluid may suit image-guided percutaneous drainage. The question principally asks **recognition and urgency**, not a long procedural description.
rubric: Covers asymptomatic, gradual and acute presentations
Lists breathlessness/orthopnoea and systemic low-output symptoms

items.title: 2011.1 Q4: Human albumin for perioperative volume replacement
items.q: Evaluate the use of human albumin in perioperative volume replacement.
items.model:
> **Examiner report verified:** 2011.1 Q4, pass rate 11%. The report requires properties, advantages/disadvantages, critical evaluation of evidence including SAFE/meta-analyses, and perioperative context. It is not an official model answer. Contemporary evidence is distinguished below.

## Properties and role

Human albumin is a **plasma-derived colloid** (4–5% approximately iso-oncotic or 20–25% concentrated/hyperoncotic), molecular mass ~66 kDa and a major contributor to plasma oncotic pressure. It binds endogenous substances and drugs and has non-oncotic biological functions. Its immediate plasma-expanding effect depends on **endothelial permeability, vascular tone and the underlying illness**: retention is **unpredictable in capillary leak**. Hyperoncotic albumin may expand plasma volume, but sustained interstitial reabsorption is limited under the revised Starling model; neither oedema mobilisation nor improved tissue perfusion is guaranteed.

## Advantages

- May provide greater **intravascular expansion per administered volume** than crystalloid in selected conditions, although this advantage varies with capillary permeability.
- Avoids the established renal/coagulation harms associated with **hydroxyethyl starch** in critically ill patients; infusion reactions are still possible.
- Has established **specific cirrhosis-related indications**, particularly after large-volume paracentesis and certain complications, according to relevant protocols.

## Disadvantages

- **Cost** and limited supply; pooled human product (small theoretical infection or prion risk).
- No demonstrated overall survival advantage over appropriate crystalloid in most general resuscitation populations; **fluid overload/pulmonary oedema** are still possible.
- Hyperoncotic formulations may redistribute fluid and require monitoring; acute TBI is an important harm signal. Product choice must take renal/cardiac function, sodium content, patient preference and availability into account.

## Evidence (and its quality)

- **SAFE** (~7000 ICU patients, 4% albumin versus saline): no overall mortality advantage; secondary TBI analyses found harm with albumin. The severe-sepsis subgroup signal is not proof of benefit. Extrapolation from ICU to perioperative care is imperfect.
- **ALBIOS** (20% albumin in severe sepsis): no overall mortality benefit; subgroup findings are uncertain.
- Systematic reviews have not established a general survival advantage for albumin over crystalloids. **2026 SSC** conditionally favours crystalloids alone over routine supplemental albumin in sepsis/shock, while permitting selected use after large crystalloid volumes or with cirrhosis.
- **Large-volume paracentesis** has a specific evidence-based indication. Do not present cardiac-surgery circuit priming or perioperative hypoalbuminaemia as proof of a universal albumin outcome benefit.

## Perioperative settings

- **Haemorrhage/obstetrics/trauma:** haemostasis and appropriate blood components restore oxygen carriage and haemostasis; albumin does not replace either function.
- **Cardiac surgery:** may reduce crystalloid volume, but routine priming or volume replacement has not established a general clinical-outcome advantage; consider bleeding, renal risk and cost.
- **Burns/capillary leak:** volume-sparing use is context-specific; timing and specialist protocols matter. It is not a universal survival-improving intervention.
- **Liver disease/transplantation:** distinguish specific cirrhosis indications from routine replacement during an operation. Hypoalbuminaemia alone does not establish benefit from correction.
- **Sepsis:** selected supplemental use after substantial crystalloid exposure, rather than routine first-line administration. **Avoid in TBI**.

This addresses the report's request for clinical evaluation across perioperative settings without implying benefit in each setting.

## Conclusion

Albumin is an **expensive, selectively useful colloid**, not a universally effective or risk-free volume expander. Use **appropriate crystalloid first** for most non-haemorrhagic volume resuscitation; reserve albumin for evidence-supported indications or individually justified cases, while accounting for capillary leak/overload and **avoiding it in TBI**.

items.title: 2010.2 Q5: Fluid management of an infant with intussusception
items.q: A 6-month-old boy presents with an acute abdomen. He is diagnosed with intussusception and booked for laparotomy after a failed attempt at reduction. His heart rate is 160bpm and BP is 75/45 mmHg. His electrolyte profile is as shown: sodium 132 mmol/l (135 – 145), potassium 2.7 mmol/l (3.5 – 5.5), chloride 106 mmol/l (95 – 110), urea 3.3 mmol/l (3.5 – 8.5), creatinine 86 µmol/l (60 – 110), lactate 4.5 mmol/l (1.0 – 1.8). (a) How would you determine his degree of dehydration and how severe is it likely to be? (40%) (b) Describe your perioperative fluid management. (40%) (c) When would you proceed to surgery and why? (20%)
items.model:
> **Examiner report verified:** 2010.2 Q5, pass rate 65.5%. Priorities are age-appropriate interpretation, shock versus dehydration, correct maintenance arithmetic/fluid choice, and reasoned operative timing. Historical practice and contemporary safety requirements are distinguished below.

## (a) Degree of dehydration (40%)

- **History**: duration of vomiting, bilious or not, red-currant jelly stool, oral intake, urine output (nappies), lethargy.
- **Examination**: weight (versus baseline), conscious state and irritability, **capillary refill (over 2 to 3 seconds)**, skin turgor, sunken fontanelle and eyes, dry mucous membranes, peripheries, and the **trend** in heart rate and blood pressure.
- **Investigations:** lactate **4.5 mmol/L** is concerning but nonspecific; sodium 132 and **potassium 2.7 mmol/L** require assessment/monitoring. A creatinine of **86 μmol/L must be interpreted using an infant-specific reference interval** and trend—not the adult-like printed range (60–110) or assumed normal renal function. Obtain glucose, blood gas/base excess, serial electrolytes and urine output.
- **Severity:** HR 160 and BP 75/45 may be compatible with distress and age-related physiology, but **do not exclude compensated shock** in a 6-month-old. Examine CRT, pulse volume, extremity temperature, mentation, weight trend and urine; estimate dehydration from the full picture rather than declaring a precise 5–10% deficit from the stem alone.

## (b) Fluid management (40%)

- **Resuscitation:** IV/IO access and isotonic crystalloid in appropriately sized **10 mL/kg aliquots**, reassessing perfusion; larger or repeated aliquots depend on ongoing losses, heart function, sepsis/obstruction and local paediatric guidance. Blood if haemorrhage is present.
- **Deficit:** estimate from recent weight change and clinical findings; **deficit (mL) = percentage dehydration × weight (kg) × 10** when percentage is written as a whole number. For example, an estimated 5% deficit in a 7-kg infant is 350 mL, not a diagnosis supplied by the stem. Subtract fluid already received and replace according to sodium, perfusion and urgency. Do not enforce a universal “half in eight hours” timetable.
- **Maintenance:** explain the **4–2–1 rule** (for a hypothetical 7–8 kg infant, 28–32 mL/h) but prescribe **balanced isotonic intraoperative maintenance fluid**, adding **1–2% glucose when hypoglycaemia risk warrants it** (this acutely unwell infant needs serial glucose). Postoperatively, use the local isotonic/glucose regimen and reassess rate, losses and stress-related ADH; avoid automatically continuing full maintenance. Healthy older children having short operations do not all require glucose supplementation.
- **Ongoing losses:** **measure** NG/stool/operative losses and replace their water and electrolyte content separately; do not assume a fixed “third-space” mL/kg/h.
- **Potassium:** K 2.7 mmol/L requires ECG, repeated biochemistry, renal function/urine assessment and correction of Mg. With bowel obstruction, IV replacement may be needed: an example RCH ward regimen is **0.2 mmol/kg/h for 3 h (maximum 10 mmol/h)**, with an infusion pump, ECG monitoring for K <3, and repeat K before further replacement. This is an example, not a universal prescription: renal dysfunction and perioperative urgency require paediatric/ICU input and local concentration/access limits. Never give an IV potassium bolus.
- **Intraop:** titrate to measured losses and perfusion; monitor HR/BP/CRT, glucose, gas, Hb, electrolytes and temperature.
- **Postop:** assess ongoing NG losses, renal function and fluid accumulation; use isotonic maintenance/glucose appropriate to risk, consider a reduced basal rate with postoperative ADH, and return to enteral intake when feasible. Monitor urine output (often aiming around 1 mL/kg/h in this infant, interpreted with the full clinical picture), weight and serial biochemistry.

## (c) Timing of surgery (20%)

Proceed **after immediate resuscitation has improved perfusion and dangerous correctable abnormalities have been addressed as far as time allows**, with a coordinated anaesthetic/surgical plan. No fixed **1–2-hour** waiting period is justified. If perforation, bowel ischaemia or peritonitis is suspected, do not delay time-critical source control: continue resuscitation **during transfer and surgery**, with appropriate monitoring and ICU support.

> **Examiner-focused point:** Allocate time 40% assessment / 40% fluid plan / 20% timing. Distinguish child-specific reference ranges and perfusion findings, name the isotonic fluid/glucose strategy, and avoid unmonitored potassium or unmeasured “third-space” replacement.
